govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Ireland brought a resolution to the United Nations in the late 1950s urging that nuclear weapons not spread to more countries. That Irish Resolution became a forerunner of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty. This briefing-book page marks the sixtieth anniversary of the Irish initiative with the Archive's records. The evidence here is the title alone, so the documents cannot be named. The subject deserves its marker: the global nonproliferation regime began partly as a small country's idea, pressed patiently year after year.

Through the 1980s, intelligence reports on Pakistan's nuclear program kept raising tension between Washington and Islamabad. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in April 2012, on newly released documents from the Reagan years. The reports suggested Pakistan was moving toward a bomb.

The tension had a second cause: Pakistan was also America's partner in supporting Afghan fighters against the Soviets. Officials had to weigh a secret weapons program against a needed alliance, year after year. The documents show that balancing in real time. It is a clean case of nonproliferation policy bending around a war Washington cared about more.

William Burr edited this briefing book, number 834, published in July 2023, on the nuclear football from Eisenhower to George W. Bush. The football's emergency action decrees were called, by American officials themselves, of doubtful legality or even illegal.

Documents show the football formally assigned to Vice President Walter Mondale, an unusual step. Pentagon officials also worried that Vice President Lyndon Johnson had not been briefed on the football at the time of Kennedy's assassination. That gap, at the moment of maximum danger, is the kind of detail only records preserve. The set follows the briefcase as an institution, president by president.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness:
President Dwight Eisenhower spoke of rolling back Soviet control of Eastern Europe, but his private conclusion was bleaker. Ronald D. Landa edited this briefing book, number 581, published in February 2017. It presents an unpublished Defense Department draft history of American attempts to keep the pot simmering in the region.

Eisenhower concluded that neither American military operations nor popular uprisings were feasible against Soviet control. CIA Director Allen Dulles agreed, saying people do not revolt in the face of tanks, artillery, and tear gas, and that revolutions now happen at the top. The documents explain the gap between liberation rhetoric and the caution that governed real policy when Hungary rose in 1956.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p: The last superpower summits were the meetings between American and Soviet leaders that closed the Cold War, above all Ronald Reagan's and George H. W. Bush's encounters with Mikhail Gorbachev. A National Security Archive briefing book page collects the Archive's work under that heading, the same name as the editors' award-winning book on those summits. The evidence here is the page capture itself rather than summit transcripts, so the entry points readers toward the Archive's larger collection on the diplomacy that ended the rivalry without a war.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Cyber: North Korea runs one of the world's most aggressive state hacking programs, funding itself through bank theft and ransomware while probing foreign networks. A National Security Archive cyber brief collects its material under the heading of North Korean cyber operations. It belongs to the Archive's Cyber Vault effort. That effort gathers the public record on state cyber activity. The evidence preserved for this entry is the page capture alone. It serves as an index point for the brief's subject. It is not a document set a reader can search directly.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cybervault_Cyber_:
American military cyber operations grew up fast and largely in secret, and a National Security Archive cyber brief gathers material on how the Department of Defense built and ran them. The brief, edited by Michael Martelle, sits inside the Archive's Cyber Vault project, which works against the overclassification of records about cyberspace.

The brief is paired with a featured article on overclassification and its impact on cyber conflict and democracy, by Jason Healey and a co-author. Their point frames the documents: when nearly everything about cyber operations is secret, the public and even policymakers cannot judge the risks. Readers get both primary material on defense cyber work and a clear argument for why so much of it stays hidden, and what that secrecy costs.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Guatema:
Guatemala's Historical Archive of the National Police, known as the AHPN, holds millions of records from the country's civil war years and has been used to prosecute human rights crimes. In August 2018, the National Security Archive reported the archive in crisis: its director, Gustavo Meono Brenner, had been abruptly removed by the Guatemalan government.

The removal was one of several moves the Archive said the government and a United Nations office had arranged together. More than fifty remaining staff were put on temporary contracts. Control of the archive also moved, from the national archives, where it had sat since 2009, to the Ministry of Culture and Sports. For readers, the posting shows how an archive can be weakened without being closed, by changing its leadership, its staff terms, and its chain of command.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_southern-cone_Dec: The Trump administration agreed to hand Argentina a trove of declassified American records. They concern the human rights violations of its 1976 to 1983 military dictatorship. A National Security Archive briefing book page announces that turnover. Its headline spells out the whole transaction. Such releases give Argentine courts and families American intelligence files on the junta's crimes, evidence gathered by the government that once worked with the generals. Only the page capture survives here, marking the promise whose fulfillment companion postings describe.
hebbel-agnes-bernauer:
A bathhouse keeper's daughter marries Duke Albrecht of Bavaria in secret, and his father orders her drowned as a witch. Hebbel's Agnes Bernauer, given here in German, builds its tragedy on a true fifteenth-century story. Love stands against reason of state, and the state wins by murder.

Agnes herself barely resists; the horror lies in the calm logic that condemns her. Counselors argue necessity, and necessity grinds pity to dust. Hebbel called such collisions the real subject of tragedy, and this play proves his theory. It remains his most moving work for many readers. The drowning at Straubing still echoes through German memory and drama.
her-father-s-daughter: A novel by Gene Stratton-Porter about a girl shaped by her father's values, set against the author's beloved Indiana nature. Family loyalty, young love, and the moral lessons of the outdoors weave through the story in Stratton-Porter's warm, earnest style. Wholesome fiction from one of America's best-selling authors.
heu-heu-or-the-monster: Heu-Heu, or The Monster, H. Rider Haggard's African tale. The monster's story. This book preserves that adventure. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
hiram-the-young-farmer: Burbank L. Todd's novel about Hiram, a young man learning the farmer's trade in early-1900s America. Hard work, country wisdom, and young love fill a story written to inspire rural youth. Wholesome, earnest fiction from the age when farming was the nation's backbone.
homer-iliad-butler:
Homer's Iliad, composed around the eighth century BCE, stands at the head of Western literature. Samuel Butler translated the epic into plain English prose. The poem covers a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War.

Achilles, insulted by King Agamemnon, withdraws from battle in anger. His friend Patroclus fights in his place and is killed by Hector. Grief drives Achilles back to battle and to Hector's death. Butler believed prose served Homer better than forced English verse. His clear version won many readers. Pride, rage, and pity drive the oldest epic we have.
homer-odyssey-butler:
Homer's Odyssey follows the Iliad as the second great epic of ancient Greece. Samuel Butler translated it into straightforward English prose. Odysseus has fought at Troy and now struggles to get home.

Ten years of wandering bring him monsters, storms, and tempting islands. He outwits the Cyclops, resists the Sirens, and loses every companion. Meanwhile his wife Penelope holds off suitors in Ithaca with patient cunning. Butler argued, unusually, that the poem's author might have been a woman. His prose stays brisk and lucid. The voyage remains the pattern for adventure stories everywhere.
hopes-and-fears-or-scenes-from-the-life-: Hopes and Fears, or scenes from the life of a spinster, by Charlotte Yonge. The single woman's tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
huntingtower: Huntingtower, John Buchan's adventure. The tower's secret. This book preserves that novel. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
in-camp-on-the-big-sunflower: Lawrence Leslie's boys' camping story follows young campers on the Big Sunflower — their adventures, mishaps, and the lessons of outdoor life. Wholesome early-twentieth-century fun for young readers who loved the great outdoors. A cheerful period piece of American boyhood.
in-the-quarter: Robert Chambers — later famous for The King in Yellow — sets this early novel among American art students in Paris's Latin Quarter. Studios, cafés, and young love fill a story drawn from his own student days. A romantic glimpse of bohemian Paris in the 1890s.
indian-summer: William Dean Howells' Indian Summer follows middle-aged lovers to Florence for a second chance at happiness. His delicate comedy of mature romance is a quiet masterpiece. Howells at his most tender. Venice's canals mirror his lovers' tender second spring.
introduction-to-the-compleat-angler: Andrew Lang's introduction to Walton's Compleat Angler: the scholar-angler on the classic of fishing. Erudite and affectionate, it is the perfect preface. For lovers of Walton and of Lang. Lang on Walton is a meeting of kindred spirits.
isaac-bickerstaff-physician-and-astrolog: Steele invented Mr. Bickerstaff, who foretold a quack doctor’s death and then reported it with glee. All London laughed, and the Tatler was born. A neat hoax, and the start of something big. A neat hoax that made journalism history.
jack-archer: Jack Archer, G, a. Henty's Crimean War tale, the young soldier. This book preserves that historical novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
jane-oglander: Jane Oglander, Marie Belloc Lowndes's novel. Jane's tale. This book preserves that story. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
janice-day-the-young-homemaker: Helen Beecher Long's Janice Day: the young homemaker's story, wholesome and inspiring. Domestic wisdom for girls, in the popular style. A favorite of young readers. Long's Janice is a model for young homemakers, and a generation of girls took her to heart.
jezebel-s-daughter:
Jezebel's Daughter is a novel by Wilkie Collins, the English master of the sensation story. The sample opens with Collins's own letter to his Italian translator, Alberto Caccia. There he explains that this book is not the planned sequel to The Fallen Leaves. That sequel had to wait, he says, until the first part reached the widest body of readers.

Collins also defends his freedom to treat social topics that some English readers called forbidden. A novelist, he argues, deserves the same liberty as a newspaper writer or a preacher. He trusts time and a growing audience to judge his work fairly. That defiant preface frames the novel that follows, from a writer who refused to let critics fence in his art.
john-leech-s-pictures-of-life-and-charac:
John Leech's Pictures of Life and Character is William Makepeace Thackeray's essay on his friend Leech, the Punch artist. It first appeared in the Quarterly Review in December 1854. Thackeray begins by remembering the gloomy picture galleries of his own childhood. Boydell's Shakespeare prints, he says, were black and ghastly, full of staring eyes and pointing fingers.

Against those horrors he sets Leech's cheerful drawings of everyday Victorian life. The essay ranges over waxworks, worsted pictures, and West's gallery for contrast. Leech's hunters, dandies, and schoolboys caught life as it was lived around him. Thackeray writes as one artist honoring another, with warmth and long knowledge of the man. The piece stands as both criticism and friendship's tribute.
john-ward-preacher:
John Ward, Preacher is a novel by Margaret Deland, first copyrighted in 1888. Deland dedicates it to Lorin Deland, calling the book already more his than hers. A line from Omar Khayyam stands at the front: the soul that sought heaven and hell found both in itself. The story opens at Ashurst rectory, the evening before Helen Jeffrey's wedding day.

A wedding is rare excitement in Ashurst, which prides itself on being half asleep. Dr. Howe jokes that the last wedding came twelve years before. Against this quiet setting Deland sets her title figure, the new preacher whose presence stirs the parish. The opening calm is deliberate: a household in the garden, suppressed excitement, and a rector counting quiet years.
jonas-on-a-farm-in-winter:
Jonas on a Farm in Winter is a children's book by Jacob Abbott, author of the Rollo books. This edition carries the date 1851 in Roman numerals. Abbott explains in his preface that the book continues a series begun with Jonas's Stories and Jonas a Judge. A companion volume covers Jonas on a farm in summer.

Abbott says the books aim to amuse young readers and to teach them at the same time. They show honest integrity and plain practical good sense at work in childhood's ordinary life. The early chapters are named Morning, Commanding and Obeying, and Franco. Farm work in winter gives Abbott his scenes for lessons in obedience, judgment, and steady conduct.
kate-bonnet-the-romance-of-a-pirate-s-da:
Kate Bonnet: The Romance of a Pirate's Daughter is a novel by Frank R. Stockton, issued at New York in 1902. A. J. Keller and H. S. Potter drew the pictures. One caption quotes Dickory telling Kate about a wonderful pirate fight he saw. The opening chapters bring two young people, a ship, and a fish together.

A fruit-basket and a friend, two clocks, and a pair of shoes and stockings fill the next chapter titles. Kate plans, in chapter seven's plain title. Stockton, famed for gentle humor in stories like The Lady or the Tiger, here turns to the sea. His pirate's daughter promises a lighter, kinder sort of pirate romance, told with his usual dry wit.
kepler:
Kepler is Walter W. Bryant's short life of the astronomer Johannes Kepler, in the Pioneers of Progress series of 1920. Bryant wrote from the Royal Observatory at Greenwich. His chapters open with astronomy before Kepler, from Chaldaean eclipse prediction to Greek star lore. Early life, university days, and Kepler's turn to astronomy follow.

The central chapters bring Kepler to Tycho Brahe, the great observer whose data he inherited. Kepler's laws of planetary motion get a chapter of their own. Closing chapters cover his last years, with lists of dates, books, and a glossary for young readers. Bryant explains hard astronomy in plain stages, as befits a series for schools. The book honors the man who found how the planets truly move.
kernel-cob-and-little-miss-sweetclover:
Kernel Cob and Little Miss Sweetclover is a children's book by George Mitchell, illustrated by Tony Sarg, from 1918. Mitchell dedicates it to four named children: Ursula, Dordie, Hutch, and Bob. The story opens with Jackie and his sister Peggs, who live with their aunt. She is very old, Jackie thinks: maybe thirty-two.

The aunt, busy with her own affairs, has forgotten that children need playthings. The house holds no soldiers, dolls, animals, engines, or picture books. So the children make believe, turning their small garden into a world of pies and adventures. Kernel Cob and Miss Sweetclover, figures of their invention, lead the play. Mitchell writes a gentle tale of imagination making riches out of nothing.
king-winter:
King Winter is a short verse tale for children, printed by Gustav W. Seitz of Hamburg. No author is named. The story begins on a cold, grey day, when frost makes each step ring on the ground.

A mother sits by the fire with her children around her knees. They beg her for a story about King Winter and Jack Frost, his helper. She tells how King Winter lives far north in the Frozen Zone. He holds court in a snow palace and sits on an icy throne. Simple rhymes and pictures carry the lesson about the cold season. Children learn the north, frost, and snow through a family scene.
lady-rose-s-daughter:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published her novel Lady Rose's Daughter in 1903. Howard Chandler Christy drew its pictures. Ward was already known for Eleanor and Robert Elsmere.

Picture captions hint at the drama inside. Lady Henry gasps and falls back in her chair in one scene. Sir Wilfrid makes a firm promise in another. An older man speaks gently of Rose's child near the end. The daughter of Lady Rose must live under her mother's shadow. Ward turns that burden into a serious social novel. Christy's drawings stress faces and drawing room tension. Ward's plot turns on loyalty between mothers, daughters, and old friends.
left-tackle-thayer:
Ralph Henry Barbour published Left Tackle Thayer in 1915. Barbour also wrote Left-End Edwards and Left Guard Gilbert. Charles M. Relyea drew the pictures for this school story.

A new boy arrives at Brimfield school in the first chapter. Captain Innes, practice cuts, and a runaway wheel follow. A mysterious auto and buried treasure widen the plot beyond football. Brimfield meets defeat before the season resolves. Barbour's sports tales mixed school honor, friendship, and hard games for boy readers. Clint Thayer's school career continues Barbour's Brimfield series. Games matter, but character tests decide the real wins.
legends-of-vancouver:
E. Pauline Johnson, also called Tekahionwake, wrote Legends of Vancouver. A preface praises a poet who honors the city's Native heritage. Committee members helped her push the book through the press.

Johnson retold Squamish and other coastal legends in English prose. Mountains, inlets, and islands around Vancouver carry the stories. She heard many tales from Chief Joe Capilano, her friend. Her retellings join Indigenous tradition with her own poet's voice. The book remains a beloved part of Vancouver's literary identity. Two Brothers and the Siwash Rock appear among its tales. Johnson's Mohawk heritage shaped her telling of coast stories.
letters-from-mesopotamia-in-1915-and-jan:
Robert Palmer's letters from Mesopotamia cover 1915 and January 1916. The book was printed for private circulation only. Its title page records that Palmer was killed at the battle of Um el Hannah, aged twenty-seven.

Palmer went out with a draft from the 6th Hants to reinforce the 4th Hants. His regiment had been in India since November 1914. His letters home describe service in the Mesopotamian campaign of the First World War. A poem on war's evils stands at the front. Family printing preserved a young officer's voice that the war cut short. Private printing kept the book within family and friends. Such memorial volumes preserved many soldiers' letters that newspapers never saw.
letters-of-a-woman-homesteader:
Elinore Pruitt Stewart's Letters of a Woman Homesteader appeared in 1914. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York. A publishers' note introduces Stewart's hard road to Wyoming.

She lost her husband in a railroad accident, the note says. Left with a two-year-old daughter, she worked in Denver as a cleaner and laundress. Then she took work as a housekeeper and claimed a homestead. Her letters turn that rough life into cheerful, funny reports. Readers meet a widow who built a new life on the frontier. Her humor turns drudgery into a kind of triumph. Stewart later wrote more letters from her Wyoming ranch life.
life-of-abraham-lincoln-little-blue-book:
John Hugh Bowers wrote this short life of Abraham Lincoln in 1922. Haldeman-Julius issued it as Little Blue Book Number 324. The ten cent pocket series came from Girard, Kansas. Bowers taught history at the State Teachers' College in Pittsburg, Kansas.

His opening praises Lincoln's rise from humble beginnings by honest effort. The log cabin, rail-splitting ax, and few borrowed books appear early. Studying by pine-knot light formed the boy's character, Bowers argues. Great suffering, he writes, taught Lincoln great sympathy for others. A flatboat trip to New Orleans widened the young Lincoln's world. The slave mart at New Orleans revolted his sympathetic soul, Bowers writes.
life-of-daniel-boone-the-great-western-h:
Cecil B. Hartley wrote this life of Daniel Boone, frontiersman. Boone appears as the great western hunter and first settler of Kentucky. The book adds Boone's own autobiography, dictated by himself. Boone believed he was ordained to settle the wilderness.

Early chapters trace his grandfather's emigration to Bucks County, Pennsylvania. Boone's boyhood, brief schooling, and a terminating anecdote follow. The family then removes to North Carolina's Yadkin River country. Indian adventures and border hazards fill the career that follows. Byron's verse describes the Yadkin country Boone entered as a boy. His grandfather first settled the family in Bucks County.
life-of-father-hecker:
The Reverend Walter Elliott wrote this life of Father Hecker in 1891. The Columbus Press published it in New York. Archbishop Corrigan granted the book its official imprimatur. Elliott calls himself Hecker's first biographer in the preface.

He writes with the joy of a son, he confesses. Hecker's own journals, letters, and recorded sayings dominate the book. Elliott reckons Hecker has three words here to his one. His own words, he says, are merely hinges and latches. Archbishop Hewit served as censor deputatus for the edition. Hecker's recorded sayings, Elliott hopes, swing open heaven-made wisdom.
life-of-luther:
Julius Köstlin wrote this life of Luther, translated from German. A Cranach portrait in Weimar's town church fronts the volume. Köstlin calls Luther Germany's most powerful religious influence. No German, he argues, so faithfully mirrored his people's character.

His larger two-volume work of 1875 gathered the full materials. That study supplied references, historical and critical, for this life. Protestants read Luther with love and veneration, Köstlin writes. Others treat him as a rock of offence, he admits candidly. Cranach's portrait comes from Weimar's town church collection. Köstlin's dedication borrows Luther's praise of a god-fearing, home-keeping wife.
lightfoot-the-deer:
Thornton W. Burgess tells children the story of Lightfoot the deer. Peter Rabbit meets Lightfoot in the opening chapter. Lightfoot explains how his new antlers grew. Sammy Jay soon brings him word of danger.

A long game of hide and seek with a hunter follows. Paddy the Beaver becomes Lightfoot's partner in escaping danger. Hounds pursue him until a long swim shakes them off. The hunting season ends, and love arrives with a stranger deer. Visitors come to Paddy's pond as the watcher chapters multiply. A great fight and an unseen watcher precede the surprising discovery.
lives-of-john-donne-henry-wotton-rich-d-:
Izaak Walton's second volume of lives opens with Richard Hooker. This issue rests on John Major's edition of 1825. Major printed from the 1675 edition, corrected by Walton's own pen. Austin Dobson added marginalia and supplementary notes later.

Hooker authored the learned Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity. A friend persuaded Walton to write his life, he says. George Herbert, prebendary of Salisbury, receives the next life. Dr. Robert Sanderson, Bishop of Lincoln, closes the volume. Cowper's verse praises Hooker's lasting monument in his books. I. G. dated the editorial note on Walton's birthday, 1898.
london-pride-or-when-the-world-was-young:
M. E. Braddon published this historical novel in 1896. She had written Lady Audley's Secret, Vixen, and Ishmael before. Chapter One, A Harbour from the Storm, opens the contents. Within Convent Walls and Letters from Home follow.

A bitter winter opens the tale in the Royal tragedy's year. Sleet rattles against an old leathern coach at dusk. Puritan houses, priest's holes, and King's Bench courts await inside. Fashion's top and London-Oxford roads carry the historical action. Dido, Philaster, and the Millbank ghost haunt the contents. High stakes and King's Bench revelations drive the later chapters.
london-river:
H. M. Tomlinson published these Thames essays in 1921. Knopf and Garden City Publishing issued the volume. He dedicates it to his mother and his father's memory. The Foreshore opens the contents on the City's north side.

Poverty Corner begins a shipping parish invisible to strangers. A midnight voyage and the ship-runners follow the river down. An old Lloyd's Register closes the collection. Tomlinson finds deep water memories hidden inside ordinary Fenchurch Street. Seamen alone use Poverty Corner's name among themselves, Tomlinson notes. A stranger lighting a pipe there might guess nothing of it.
love-letters-between-a-nobleman-and-his-:
Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister is an early novel by Aphra Behn. Behn was among the first English women to earn her living by writing. Her story is told in letters between lovers caught in scandal. The argument here sets part of the tale amid the Huguenot wars in France.

There a young nobleman serves under the Prince of Condé, here called Cesario. He loves Myrtilla, a lady famed for beauty, youth, and wit. Love, flight, and court intrigue drive the letters forward. Behn mixed real scandal with romance and politics. Her book helped shape the young English novel. It still reads as bold, lively, and ahead of its time.
love-the-fiddler:
Love, the Fiddler is a book of short stories by Lloyd Osbourne. The first tale, 'The Chief Engineer,' opens on Commonwealth Street. Frank Rignold loves Florence Fenacre, a widow's daughter, with all his heart. Yet Florence, though she has never said no, will not say yes.

Other stories tell of Ffrenches First, golden castaways, and the mascot of Battery B. Osbourne mixes love tales with sea and adventure yarns. He learned storytelling beside his stepfather, Robert Louis Stevenson. His manner is warm, clear, and full of incident. The book shows love as a fiddler, calling the tune for all.
maori-and-settler:
Maori and Settler is G. A. Henty's story of the New Zealand War, dated 1891. It stands in his famous uniform series of boys' histories. Shelf-mates tell of Nelson, the Dutch revolt, and ancient Egypt. Eminent artists illustrated the whole set of volumes.

An English settler family faces the perils of colonizing New Zealand. War with the Maori brings raids, alarms, and hard choices. Henty builds his tale from the colony's real struggles. His young heroes learn courage amid bush and battlefield. The book taught Victorian boys the empire's far frontiers. It is both an adventure story and a period document. Readers see the colonial past through its own eyes.
marco-polo-travels-yule-cordier:
Marco Polo dictated his account of Asia after returning to Venice from years in Kublai Khan's service. Henry Yule translated the book, and Henri Cordier later revised Yule's great edition. Their Yule-Cordier text, the standard English version, is the one given here in its 1920 form.

Polo describes the Khan's court, paper money, coal, and cities larger than any in Europe. His marvels drew doubt in his own day and wonder ever since. Yule's notes turn the tale into a library of Asian geography and history. The Travels redrew the mental maps of the West. No medieval travel book has matched its reach or its fame.
martin-hyde-the-duke-s-messenger:
Martin Hyde, the Duke's Messenger is John Masefield's 1910 tale for young readers. Martin tells his own story, starting with four tries at leaving home. At last he goes to sea and finds his friend.

Chapters move from sea life to Aurelia and brave Captain Barlow. Then come the road to Lyme, the landing, and a voice at dawn. Masefield, a poet and sailor, gives the Monmouth rising of 1685 a boy's eye view. The heads promise sounds in the night and a drink of sherbet. Young readers get war and sea risk told close to a boy's fears.
martin-rattler:
R. M. Ballantyne published Martin Rattler in 1858. Martin lives with his aunt, Mrs. Dorothy Grumbit, in Ashford. She calls him a very bad boy, and the bane of her life.

Yet the whole village smiles when Martin comes by. The vicar calls him full of fun, and sure to mend with age. Ballantyne draws a rosy, bright eyed lad whose tricks hide a warm and brave heart. His dark brown eyes light with fun the moment he wakes. Ballantyne sets up a hero whose faults are mostly high spirits. The doctor alone calls him a scamp, and means it.
marzio-s-crucifix-and-zoroaster:
F. Marion Crawford paired two tales in Marzio's Crucifix and Zoroaster. P. F. Collier and Son issued the book in New York in 1887. It forms one part of his novels in twenty five volumes.

Marzio's Crucifix opens in a silver shop in Rome. Marzio Pandolfi rails that modern life is a living lie. His apprentice, Gianbattista Bordogni, works on fine carved silver as he talks. Craft, faith, and temper clash in the small, bright work room. The second tale bears the name of the old Persian prophet. Pairing a Roman craft tale with that tale gives the book wide range.
mcguffey-s-fifth-eclectic-reader:
McGuffey's Fifth Eclectic Reader stands high in the revised school set. Its rights run from 1879 to 1920 in this copy. The preface says the book grew larger in the new form.

New pieces came in only where the gain was clear and sure. The editors sought a wide range of top authors and fine style. Notes explain hard parts, since most pupils lacked reference books. Word lists give the sense and sound of the tough terms in each lesson. First drills in clear speech and tone stand before the lessons. Health in morals was a stated aim, not a side effect.
mcguffey-s-fourth-eclectic-reader:
McGuffey's Fourth Eclectic Reader is the fourth step in the revised set. Its transcriber notes the plain moral tone of the schoolroom of 1900. Old forms, like do n't with a space, stand as printed.

The editors kept the core traits of the McGuffey books intact. New pieces replaced old ones only where the gain was plain. Prose and verse lessons train both skill and conduct. Section numbers shift from decimal in the contents to Roman in the body. Page heads are cut in this copy, but page numbers stay with each head. That choice keeps the text clean for class use.
mcguffey-s-second-eclectic-reader:
McGuffey's Second Eclectic Reader, revised, is the second step in the set. Rights in this copy run from 1879 to 1920. Lessons in prose and poetry fill the book for young pupils.

Evening at Home leads, and Bubbles comes second in the list. Willie's Letter appears in script for children to read. The Little Star, Two Dogs, and Afraid in the Dark follow. First drills in sounds and punctuation marks stand at the front. The heads move from home scenes to small tales of fear and fun. Short pieces keep new readers from tiring too fast.
mcguffey-s-sixth-eclectic-reader:
McGuffey's Sixth Eclectic Reader tops the revised school set. A front picture shows a young woman by a trunk, finger raised. The caption quotes item ninety five, Ginevra, with the word beware.

Many pieces carry a short life of their author at the head. Such lives end with a mark of three pound signs in this copy. The lessons aim at older pupils with harder prose and verse. Its copyist notes the same plain moral tone as the lower books. The raised finger in the picture warns of a tale's turn. Older pupils were trusted with longer, harder set pieces.
mcguffey-s-third-eclectic-reader:
McGuffey's Third Eclectic Reader, revised, sits mid way in the set. Its long run of fame is praised on the rights page. Parts of the book use marks with no plain text match.

Those parts stand as pictures, with text set beside them as a guide. Script pieces appear in the same paired form for young eyes. Old spellings, like do n't with a space, are kept as printed. The book trains pupils who have cleared the first two readers. The copyist flags that much of the charm sits in the marks. Print and script side by side train eye and hand at once.
melmoth-the-wanderer:
Charles Robert Maturin, an Irish priest, wrote this vast Gothic tale in 1820. It was his last book, and the work that made his name last. Maturin wrote in a wild, high style that Balzac and Baudelaire prized in the years to come.

Melmoth has sold his soul for a span of a hundred and fifty years of life. He roams the world to find a soul in such pain that it will take his pact in his place. None will, and his doom rolls on. The book is the last great work of the Gothic line.
memoirs-of-the-comtesse-du-barry-with-mi:
Baron Etienne Leon Lamothe-Langon wrote the Memoirs of the Comtesse Du Barry. The title claims the book was written by herself, in quotes. A special intro by Robert Arnot heads this edition.

A note warns that the claim of her own hand is a pose. Lamothe-Langon, who lived from 1786 to 1864, made her voice himself. Her tale starts in mid action, with a letter from Lebel. An invite to sup with Louis XV, and coaching from Comte Jean, follow. The tale breaks off at both ends, the note warns readers. That lack gives it the feel of a found diary slice.
men-called-him-master:
Elwyn Allen Smith wrote this life of Jesus, published by the Westminster Press in Philadelphia in 1948. The book retells the Gospel story in plain modern chapters. Its title comes from the respect Jesus's followers showed him as their teacher and lord. Smith writes for general readers, not scholars.

Chapters move from John the Baptist's voice in the wilderness to the calling of the first disciples. They cover Jesus's teaching about the kingdom of God and the mission of his followers. Questions at the start invite readers to wonder along with the story. The book offers a clear, devout retelling of the New Testament account.
meyer-us4421474-hydrogen-gas-burner:
Stanley A Meyer received United States Patent 4,421,474 on December 20, 1983, for a hydrogen gas burner. The filing belongs to his water fuel cell family, eight patents strong in this set. Meyer said water could be split cheaply and the gas burned for heat.

The burner patent describes the head, the gas feed, and the flame control for his hydrogen mix. It was meant to turn his fuel gas into steady, useful heat for homes or shops. A patent records a claimed design, not a working proof. An Ohio court ruled Meyer's claims fraudulent in 1996.
meyer-us4465455-start-up-shut-down-for-a:
United States Patent 4,465,455, granted to Stanley A Meyer on August 14, 1984, covers the start-up and shut-down system for his hydrogen gas burner. It is a control patent inside his eight-part water fuel cell family. Safe starts and stops were key to his promised home heating unit.

The filing lays out the valves, switches, and order of steps for lighting the burner and cutting it off. Hydrogen burns fast and can flash back, so the controls guard each stage. Patents show a design was filed as new, not that it worked. Meyer's claims were found fraudulent in an Ohio court in 1996.
michael-mcgrath-postmaster:
Ralph Connor set this story in the Fraser Valley of British Columbia. The narrator rides in with a pack pony, carrying a photograph kit and camping outfit. He is crossing mountain trails toward the Pacific Coast, hundreds of miles away. At the end of a hard day he meets Ould Michael, the postmaster of the title.

Connor was already known for The Sky Pilot and Black Rock when this tale appeared in 1900. The opening pages linger on fir forests, roaring creeks, and the broad river below. Michael himself fastens into the narrator's memory for life. The story blends frontier scenery with the character of a beloved local figure.
miss-ludington-s-sister:
Edward Bellamy opens this novel in Hilton, a farming village among the Massachusetts hills. Ida Ludington was the village belle, idol of its young men and leader of its girls. At twenty, at the height of her beauty, she fell ill of a dreadful disease. The girl, Bellamy writes, in effect died; a sad and faded woman rose from that bed.

By twenty-five, Ida believes her happiness is finished, and only memory remains. The title's mystery is the sister of Miss Ludington, a presence touched by the supernatural. Bellamy, later famous for Looking Backward, builds a tender tale of lost youth and love. The story asks what remains when beauty and hope are taken early.
mobilizing-woman-power:
Harriot Stanton Blatch published this wartime argument in 1918. She dedicates it to the women of Great Britain and France. They have stood behind the Allied armies, she writes, as an unswerving second line of defense. A frontispiece shows Joan of Arc as the spirit of the Allied women.

Chapters survey how Britain, France, and Germany each mobilized their women. America, in her account, is only beginning to send women over the top. She takes up women's pay, a land army, and pooling brains. Blatch, a leading suffragist, argues that winning the war requires women's full labor, fairly organized and fairly paid.
modern-english-books-of-power:
George Hamlin Fitch collected these essays from the Sunday book page of the San Francisco Chronicle. Barse and Hopkins published them in 1912. His epigraph comes from Milton's Areopagitica: a good book is the precious life-blood of a master spirit. A frontispiece sketch by Daniel Maclise shows Dickens reading The Chimes to friends in 1844.

Fitch surveys the English books he judged most powerful and enduring. The essays introduce great authors and their masterworks to newspaper readers. He writes as a working critic, not a professor, and keeps the tone inviting. The book preserves Edwardian popular criticism at its most enthusiastic and readable.
molly-mcdonald-a-tale-of-the-old-frontie:
Randall Parrish published this frontier tale in April 1912. A. L. Burt reprinted it at New York with four color illustrations by Ernest L. Blumenschein. The contents open with an unpleasant situation and a man called Brick Hamlin. Then come the news at Ripley and an attack.

The middle chapters defend a stagecoach and take stock of those trapped inside it. Plans for escape lead to a way to the river, and across it. Acquaintance ripens between rescuer and rescued before the parting. Parrish, author of Keith of the Border, writes the old frontier as action first and romance close behind.
montezuma-s-daughter:
H. Rider Haggard published this Aztec romance in 1893, dedicating it to his friend J. Gladwyn Jebb. Thomas Wingfield narrates his own adventures in the first person. His Spanish cousin Juan de Garcia murders his mother, and Wingfield's road runs through the Inquisition, shipwreck, and slavery. He joins a Spanish expedition to New Spain unwillingly.

Haggard's note says the portents before the Aztec Empire's fall are mainly historical. He took a prayer from Sahagún's history of New Spain, written soon after the conquest. The speech of the Emperor Guatemoc under torture is also authentic. Wingfield loves Otomie, Montezuma's daughter, amid the empire's destruction.
mother:
Owen Wister's long story first appeared anonymously in 1901, in a house-party volume by several authors. He remodelled it for separate publication in 1907. The dedication jokes to his favorite broker that Mr. Beverly is not meant for him. A house party frames the tale, as guests take turns telling stories.

Handsome young Richard Field offers no invention, but a true chapter from his own life. A lovely, innocent girl is its heroine. His wife Ethel protests: he has never confessed this episode to her. The company insists, and the middle-aged listeners lean in, hungry for a love story they can no longer live themselves.
mrs-red-pepper:
Grace Smith Richmond published this novel in 1913, a sequel to Red Pepper Burns. The contents open with a chapter called Wholly Given Over to Sentiment. Burns, the red-haired doctor, does his duty in chapter three. A crisis, a challenge, and flashlights fill later chapters.

Richmond's earlier books, like Strawberry Acres, had won her many readers. Here the doctor's wife takes the title and the heart. Talk around the apple tree and a runaway road lighten the plot. The tale blends home life, work, and love. It is warm small-town fiction, built on talk, kindness, and second thoughts.
muir-first-summer:
John Muir kept a journal in the summer of 1869, when he herded sheep into the Sierra Nevada. Published in 1911 as My First Summer in the Sierra, it became the book that made him the prophet of American wilderness. He was thirty-one and unknown.

Muir records granite domes, giant sequoias, bears, storms, and flowers with equal joy. He calls the range the Range of Light, and his delight in it fills every page. The shepherd's dull job fades behind his study of glaciers and forests. Few nature books have sent so many readers into the mountains.
my-brilliant-career:
Miles Franklin wrote this fierce first novel, dated from New South Wales in 1899. Henry Lawson sent it from England in April 1901. The narrator warns readers the story is all about herself. She makes no apology for being self-centered.

She calls the book not a romance but a real yarn. Gum trees, hardship, and bitter heartache mark its truth, she says. She hates the slow life that eats her youth and prime. Her sphere feels like a living death to her. The novel's raw voice made it a landmark of Australian writing, a young woman's cry for a larger life.
narrative-and-lyric-poems-first-series-f:
O. J. Stevenson, a professor of English in Ontario, edited this school reader. Copp, Clark of Toronto issued it in 1912, with full notes. The poems serve the lower school, as the title says. Moore's Meeting of the Water opens the contents.

Scott's Jock o' Hazeldean and Macaulay's Horatius follow. Wordsworth's Solitary Reaper and Mrs. Browning's Musical Instrument appear too. Longfellow's Builders and Miles Standish give American voices. Lowell's Vision of Sir Launfal closes the sample list. Stevenson's notes guide young readers through each tale and song. The book shows what Canadian schoolchildren once learned by heart.
narrative-of-a-voyage-to-senegal-in-1816:
J. B. Henri Savigny and Alexander Correard survived the wreck of the Medusa. Their account tells of a voyage to Senegal in 1816. The French government had ordered the trip. Of one hundred fifty people left on a raft, fifteen lived.

Thirteen days adrift stripped those fifteen of all they owned. The tale moves from the raft to the Zaara desert and St. Louis. Notes on farming along Africa's west coast close the book. Paris opened a relief fund for the saved men. Few sea tales match this one for horror, blame, and the will to live against all odds.
nasa-tm-19630010659-wind-tunnel-investig:
Albin O. Pearson of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-547. It reports tunnel tests of changed Mercury capsule shapes. The shapes were for escape and exit versions of the capsule. Speeds ran from Mach 0.30 to 1.14, through the sound barrier.

An escape capsule must fly clear of a failing rocket at once. Its shape still has to stay steady at low speed. Pearson measured the steady air forces on each changed layout. Small shape tweaks can shift balance in that slow range. The data helped engineers tune the Mercury escape system, the crew's last chance if a launch went wrong.
nasa-tm-19640019264-booster-parametric-d:
V. Verderaime of Marshall Space Flight Center's Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory wrote this memorandum, TM X-53053. It gives a parametric design method for rocket boosters. Part two, this part, treats propulsion, the engines and their layout. Parametric means designs are compared by sweeping key numbers, not by single guesses.

The abstract offers rough equations for big liquid rocket engines. Engine mass and the space an engine needs are given in flexible form. Well-known thrust equations appear with changes for booster use. The method lets teams test many booster sizes fast, on paper. It served early Saturn-era planning, where each choice shifted cost, weight, and flight path at once.
nasa-tm-19650008671-the-magnetosphere-an:
Norman F Ness of Goddard Space Flight Center gave this paper in November 1964 at a meeting in Gatlinburg, Tennessee. His topic was the magnetosphere, the magnetic region around Earth, and its boundary layer. That boundary is where Earth's field meets the flow coming from the Sun.

Ness begins with the Sun as Earth's main source of energy input. He recalls the 1930s idea that solar disturbances send out ionized gas. He then turns to what was known about the boundary itself. The paper captures early space-age thinking about the space around Earth.
nasa-tm-19660001929-a-data-compression-p:
Gerald Hogg at Goddard wrote this data compression primer in August 1965 for staff facing a flood of spacecraft data. Compression shrinks data so more of it can be sent or stored. Every bit sent from orbit cost time and power. Hogg sets out the methods in plain order, with their applications, and adds a glossary of related terms.

A primer is written for newcomers, not experts. Its job is to make a whole field usable in a few pages. Goddard handled data from many missions at once in 1965. Shared terms and shared methods kept those teams from working at cross purposes. The glossary alone shows an agency teaching itself a new craft.
nasa-tm-19660007956-introduction-to-matr:
Sheldon E Newhouse at Goddard wrote this plain introduction to a useful piece of mathematics, the generalized inverse of a matrix. Ordinary inverses work only for square matrices with full rank. Many real problems use rectangular matrices, which have none. Moore first studied the answer under one name, and Penrose later under the name Newhouse uses. The pseudo-inverse of a rectangular matrix gets special attention.

Newhouse presents the most practical and striking properties, by his own account. He writes for readers not well versed in abstract mathematics. Uses include the analysis and solution of systems of linear equations. Such systems sit under orbit work, data fitting, and much else at Goddard.
nasa-tm-19660015352-two-level-voltage-li:
N Potter and R Morrison, in Goddard's Spacecraft Technology Division, described a two level voltage limiter in January 1966. The device guards a battery while it charges. Silver-cadmium batteries, the catalog note says, need charge control of this kind. A limiter holds voltage at a set level, then shifts to a second level as the battery fills, protecting it from overcharge.

Overcharging shortens a battery's life and can damage its cells. In orbit, no one can swap a ruined battery out. Two levels give a firm charge first and a gentler finish. The contents move from introduction to the functional approach. Small circuits of this type quietly decided how long many early satellites could keep working.
nasa-tm-19660028350-a-new-four-channel-s:
Ellis E. Whiting, of the Vehicle Environment Division at NASA's Ames Research Center, describes a new instrument in this paper. The instrument watches models flying through a ballistic range at very high speed. Around each model, the air heats into a glowing cap of gas, and that light carries clues about entry heating.

Whiting's spectrometer uses the glowing gas cap itself as its light source and entrance slit. As the model flies, its motion sweeps the spectrum across the detector, scanning a broad span of wavelengths. He reports that the instrument was calibrated for both wavelength and brightness. Sample test results are included to show what it can measure.
nasa-tm-19660028523-the-task-manager:
William D. Carpenter wrote The Task Manager, a 1966 NASA memorandum about how programming work should be led. Carpenter argues that good management starts with setting proper objectives, then using people, material, and time well to reach them. Waiting for a sponsor to supply every detail, he warns, leaves a programming group idle and open to blame.

His answer is a single task manager who acts as the one point of contact between the branch and the sponsor. That person draws up specifications the sponsor can accept and the team can live with. The role keeps effort continuous and avoids costly duplicated work. Although Carpenter writes in the language of programming, he states that the principles apply to other fields as well.
nasa-tm-19670002014-an-auto-diagrammer:
G. Hain and K. Hain, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, describe a computer program that draws its own diagrams. The program, called the Auto-Diagrammer, uses the plotter of an SC 4020 computer. It was built so engineers would not have to draw flowcharts by hand.

The program draws flowcharts automatically from PERT or LOGIC data cards. It can also work straight from FORTRAN and FAP source decks, with no extra control cards. It handles large networks, and it can shrink a chart to show the overall logic more clearly. The paper gives the program's logic, operating instructions, and detailed examples.
nasa-tm-19670013552-finite-element-model:
Jerry F. Kuzanek wrote this paper at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in March 1967. It treats finite element modeling of a cantilever beam, a beam fixed at one end and free at the other. The catalog record says the work computes the beam's sideways vibration frequencies, combining bending with rotatory inertia and shear flexibility.

After a section on theoretical solutions, Kuzanek builds three computer models of the beam. Two are bending models, named for their digit schemes, and the third is a diagonal model whose shear behavior gets detailed treatment. Worked examples follow for two aluminum beams, one small and square in section and one larger and rectangular. Tables give the input prepared for a structural analysis computer program and the frequencies each model predicts for the smaller beam.
nasa-tm-19670014003-hydraulic-axisymmetr:
Fabio R. Goldschmied and Michael A. Kalange, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, wrote this memorandum on December 15, 1966. It presents hydraulic diverters, devices that switch a liquid stream on and off. The design uses an axisymmetric focused jet, controlled by air pressure rather than moving parts.

Fluidic technology, the authors note, badly needed amplifiers in the large-flow, moderate-pressure class. Their goals were fast switching without destructive water hammer, and no mechanical parts to wear. A standing cavitation bubble in the control cavity lets a pneumatic signal switch the flow. Tests of a model diverter reached useful pressure recovery and efficiency, of the order of half.
nasa-tm-19670020661-a-magnetic-core-digi:
In June 1967, NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this paper on a particle detector built for space science. The instrument is a spark chamber, which makes the paths of charged particles visible as sparks. This design reads out spark positions digitally with magnetic cores, suiting it for balloons first and ultimately for satellites.

The assembled chamber holds thirty-two active spark modules and forms the heart of a gamma-ray telescope. Each module uses two wire grids, crossing at right angles, as its electrodes. A terminating resistor on every wire localizes each discharge, giving good multiple-spark performance at low overvoltages. Lower voltages in turn sharpen spatial resolution. The builders stressed strength and long-term operation under satellite conditions. On-board data handling combines a buffered memory readout, a housekeeping multiplexer, a tape recorder, and a telemetry encoder and transmitter.
nasa-tm-19670022689-wind-tunnel-investig:
A wind-tunnel investigation at NASA measured how a possible re-entry capsule behaves when stacked on its rocket booster. The capsule was a nonlifting design, meant to fall back through the air rather than glide. Tests ran from Mach 0.60 to Mach 1.20, the range around the speed of sound.

The model was tested with and without an escape rocket and tower attached. With the tower on, the model stayed statically stable across the tests. The tower had no effect on stability or on the normal-force behavior. It did lower the axial-force values, though. Axial force near zero angle of attack rose as Mach number increased.
nasa-tm-19670029336-a-far-ultraviolet-po:
Donald F. Heath, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, describes an instrument in this 1967 paper. The instrument is a far ultraviolet polarization analyzer built for rocket use. Polarization analyzers measure how light waves are aligned, not just how bright the light is. This one measures the polarization of resonantly scattered sunlight in the upper atmosphere.

The analyzer uses eight rotating plates of lithium fluoride as its polarizing element. Filters of several crystal materials, used with a light sensor that is blind to longer wavelengths, divide the far ultraviolet into four bands. Heath gives the values the Zeeman effect predicts for ultraviolet multiplets that could contribute to the day airglow in the air of other planets. Departures from those values, he notes, can betray multiple scattering, atoms excited by impacts, or fine structure effects. The summed polarization of a multiplet also reflects the temperature of the gas.
nasa-tm-19680004338-simulation-study-of-:
George C. Winston and William H. Long, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this preprint in September 1967. It is a simulation study of a precise hybrid servo control system, one that mixes digital and analog control. The system was designed to aim an experimental optical tracking mount with extreme accuracy.

The control concept was relatively unique when work began in March 1963, and no published performance data for similar systems could be found. The team therefore simulated the design in detail on an analog computer before trusting it. The simulation indicated the concept was sound, a judgment later confirmed experimentally. Tracking accuracy came out well within the two arc second specification. Along the way, the study developed techniques for overcoming two nonlinear nuisances. One is amplifier saturation, where a signal hits its ceiling. The other is Coulomb friction in the moving parts.
nasa-tm-19680010137-gas-bearing-applicat:
W. J. Anderson surveys a quiet technology that space power depends on: gas bearings. Spinning machines for space power, called turbomachinery, need bearings that last for years without oil. A gas bearing floats the shaft on a film of gas.

Anderson opens with the rising hunger for power in space. Early satellites needed only a few watts; manned planetary missions would need vastly more. Batteries grow too heavy for such jobs, he argues. Dynamic power units, spinning generators driven by heat, must take over. He compares liquid-metal Rankine systems with gas-cycle Brayton systems, then turns to their bearings.
nasa-tm-19680010276-effect-of-cover-gas-:
Stanley G. Young and James R. Johnston, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a testing conference in Honolulu, Hawaii, in mid-1968. It studies the effect of cover gas pressures on accelerated cavitation damage. Cavitation is the hammering of collapsing bubbles in a liquid, which pits metal surfaces inside pumps and power systems.

A vibratory apparatus subjected three candidate materials to accelerated cavitation in hot liquid sodium, under argon cover gas at pressures up to four atmospheres. The materials were a stainless steel and two cobalt alloys considered for liquid metal space power systems. Raising the cover gas pressure significantly increased damage to every material at every exposure time. The ranking never changed: one cobalt alloy resisted best, the other stood in the middle, and the stainless steel resisted least. Microscopy showed undercutting, cracks through the metal grains, and subsurface deformation in all three.
nasa-tm-19680014655-fiber-reinforced-met:
J. W. Weeton and R. A. Signorelli of Lewis Research Center survey fiber reinforced metal composites in this 1968 technical paper. The paper was prepared for a refractory composite working group meeting at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. It covers work under way at Lewis on strong fibers set inside metal.

Topics include ceramic whiskers and polycrystalline ceramic fibers as reinforcing materials. The authors describe how such fibers can strengthen metals that must survive high heat. They review the state of the Lewis program and the problems still open. The survey helped engineers judge where fiber reinforced metals might serve in hot aerospace structures.
nasa-tm-19680024078-magnetospheric-conve:
J. P. Heppner of Goddard Space Flight Center infers magnetospheric convection patterns from high latitude activity in this August 1968 paper. He presented it at an aurora and airglow study institute in Norway. The paper follows his 1967 talk on high latitude magnetic disturbances at Keele, England.

That earlier work used a motion picture of disturbance vectors from twenty-five high latitude observatories. Each frame showed all stations at once in polar projection, stepping through sixteen days of data. Frame-by-frame study produced impressions and conclusions about disturbance patterns. Heppner uses that record to reason about how the magnetosphere circulates. The report record notes he also discusses the uses and limits of convection models.
nasa-tm-19690008772-spectral-studies-of-:
A December 1968 Goddard preprint, numbered X-622-68-451, reports spectral studies of sunlight reflected from fields, red tide, and kelp. A downward-looking spectrometer aboard a C-47 aircraft measured natural surfaces across near-infrared wavelengths. Green plants reflect strongly in one such band, the authors note. A satellite weather sensor watched that same band, raising a practical worry.

Could fields of green vegetation be confused with clouds, which also reflect strongly there? An earlier jet flight over the Yucatan jungle found jungles rather poor reflectors. Cultivated fields and sea vegetation, including kelp beds and red tide blooms, remained unanswered questions. The C-47 flights measured their reflected energy so the size of the problem could be judged.
nasa-tm-19690011521-effect-of-rotor-tip-:
Donald E. Holeski and Samuel M. Futral Jr. of Lewis Research Center measured how rotor tip clearance hurts turbine performance in this March 1969 memorandum. Their test article was a five-inch single-stage axial-flow turbine. The gap between rotor blade tips and the casing lets gas leak past the blades.

Efficiency fell in a straight line as tip clearance grew. Static efficiency dropped sharply across the clearance range tested, the authors report. Rotor exit flow surveys accompany the performance data. Comparisons with three reference turbines supported the results. Tip clearance effects proved larger for a reaction turbine than for an impulse turbine. Designers must hold tip gaps tight to protect efficiency.
nasa-tm-19690016934-experimental-data-fo:
Everett E. Bailey and Robert S. Ruggeri of Lewis Research Center present compressor test data in this May 1969 memorandum. Two rotors with tip speeds of 1400 feet per second ran with distorted inlet flow. Distortions came in both radial and circumferential forms, mimicking real engine intakes.

Data cover equivalent rotor speeds from half to full speed. The two rotors had design pressure ratios of about 1.6 and 1.76. Tables give inlet and discharge pressures and temperatures in radial and circumferential detail. Wall static pressures along hub and casing are included. Uniform inlet flow data allow direct comparison. The authors also discuss flow near stall, with and without distortion present.
nasa-tm-19700016061-the-development-of-a:
NASA issued this thesis study on a very small heater for thin film oxygen sensors. The work was presented as a thesis to the engineering faculty of the University of Virginia. The sensors gauge how much oxygen is in a gas by its partial pressure, a key reading inside a spacecraft cabin.

The opening chapters explain why oxygen sensing grew harder as missions grew longer. Early flights used nearly pure oxygen, chosen to keep supply gear light on the weak early rockets. Later plans mixed gases at low pressure, which raised health and fire questions that careful sensing had to watch. The study then turns to building a miniaturized heater for the sensor itself.
nasa-tm-19700022611-response-tests-of-cu:
Dennis W. Camp, Robert E. Turner, and Luke P. Gilchrist of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on May 18, 1970. It gives response tests for three common wind sensors. The sensors are the spinning cup, the vane, and the propeller types.

A wind tunnel program checked how each sensor answers changes in the wind. Slow response can hide gusts and lulls in the record. Weather stations and launch sites depend on these simple tools every day. The tests show how fast and how truly each type follows the air. Such data help users pick the right sensor for a job.
nasa-tm-19700025333-evaluation-of-the-lm:
How the lunar module guidance system would perform over five proposed landing sites is evaluated in this Houston internal note for the Apollo program. Each site had its own approach ground, and that ground held its own slopes and craters. The note reviews where the evaluation stood after a site selection board briefing in March 1967.

On descent, landing radar updates the guidance system's picture of speed and height. But the radar reads height above the local ground, so rough terrain makes those readings jump. Such jumps can trigger steering and thrust commands that waste fuel or break radar lock. The evaluation checks each site's approach terrain against that risk and outlines work still to come.
nasa-tm-19710002306-experimental-investi:
Roy C. Tew and Roland C. Fisher of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It tests a way to control condenser pressure while the SNAP-8 power system starts up. This is the first part of the study, and it treats control by inventory.

In this method, liquid mercury flows into or out of the system as needed. That flow holds the pressure level with a steady reservoir. The tests found that good control needs the condenser to run in its high inventory range, the authors state. They also tracked how the coolant flow played its part. Startup control decides whether a power system wakes up safely.
nasa-tm-19710004682-realization-theory-o:
NASA's Electronics Research Center issued this study on realization theory for rational transfer matrices. In control theory, realization means building a working system whose behavior matches a given transfer matrix. The study treats both the matrix and its built forms as one kind of algebraic object.

Both sides, the author shows, can be represented by a morphism of modules over a ring of polynomials. Such morphisms are called the fundamental algebraic objects of finite, constant linear systems. The development builds on results of Kalman, Gilbert, and Youla, with no large claim to originality. It is offered as a base for research on multivariable synthesis problems, such as decoupling, from this viewpoint.
nasa-tm-19710009388-effect-of-exit-area-:
Bernard J Blaha and Albert L Johns of the Lewis Research Center wrote this March 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2182. It reports wind tunnel tests of an auxiliary inlet ejector nozzle built for a supersonic cruise aircraft. The team varied the nozzle exit area to see how internal expansion changed performance, above all at slower subsonic cruise.

Tests ran in the Lewis eight by six foot supersonic wind tunnel. Exit shapes mimicked a hinged trailing edge flap, and two primary sizes stood for cruise and for reheated climb. At Mach 0.9, more expansion first cost about one percent of thrust. Pushing expansion further cost about ten percent more, a clear warning for nozzle design.
nasa-tm-19710022630-comparison-of-predic:
John B McDevitt of the Ames Research Center wrote this August 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,046. It checks whether simple theory can predict the hypersonic behavior of a lifting body shuttle orbiter. The test shape was Lockheed's delta body design, model LS-200-5. Wind tunnel readings came from Langley at Mach 10.4 and from Ames at Mach 7.4.

McDevitt used a standard hypersonic computer program for the basic vehicle estimates. Simpler ideas covered the control surfaces. In general, the program gave good estimates below about thirty degrees of attack. It predicted somewhat high forces at larger angles. The embedded flow approach best matched control power. Newtonian estimates also proved reasonably accurate for controls.
nasa-tm-19720008258-reentry-thermal-prot:
John W Vorreiter of the Ames Research Center tested a spacecraft insulation material in January 1972, as NASA TM X-62,100. The material, sold as Min-K 1301, insulated the power generator of the Pioneer F probe. That generator, an RTG, made electricity from radioactive heat. If the probe ever fell back to Earth, the insulation would face reentry heating. Vorreiter checked whether it would survive in the Ames arc heated wind tunnel.

Test results were reassuring at moderate heating rates. The material should ablate very little below the stated heat rate limit. He also proposed fastening the insulation pieces together. Joined pieces would cut the heat reaching the generator's source. The saving came to at least about a fifth of the total heat.
nasa-tm-19720016248-preliminary-mission-:
Byron L Swenson, Edward L Tindle, and Larry A Manning wrote this study in May 1972, as NASA TM X-2565. All three worked in the Advanced Concepts and Missions Division at Moffett Field. They laid out early designs for uncrewed orbiters of Jupiter. No spacecraft had yet orbited an outer planet. Their task was to match mission designs to the science goals. Hardware limits and launch power set the boundaries.

Each design aims to measure Jupiter and its surroundings again and again. Repeated orbits let instruments watch storms, fields, and moons over time. The report sums up the operating choices each design allows. It also lists the systems each option would require. Such studies shaped the path toward the later Galileo mission.
national-character:
N. C. Burt, pastor of the Franklin Street Presbyterian Church in Baltimore, gave this Thanksgiving discourse on November 15, 1855. John D. Toy printed it in Baltimore that same year. A letter printed up front shows church members asked Burt for a copy so it could be published.

The sermon takes national character as its theme for the holiday. Thanksgiving sermons in that era mixed thanks to God with warnings about public morals. Burt speaks as a pastor to his own flock, not as a historian. Short as it is, the piece shows how one city pulpit read the country's health in 1855.
new-national-first-reader:
Charles J. Barnes, Harlan H. Ballard, and S. Proctor Thayer made the New National First Reader for young pupils. The American Book Company issued it in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago, under an 1888 Barnes copyright. It opens the Barnes series of national readers for schools.

Its preface backs the word method as the most natural way to start reading. Words stand for things and acts, the authors say, while bare letters mean nothing to a child. A known word of fair length, like mamma, is learned as fast as a short one. Frequent reviews then fix new words in mind. Later reviews reshape them into fresh exercises to test true recall.
new-national-fourth-reader:
Charles J. Barnes and J. Marshall Hawkes made the New National Fourth Reader, dated 1884 in this copy. It belongs to the Barnes series of school readers. A front picture shows the destruction of Pompeii by Vesuvius, which hints at the range of its lessons.

Prose lessons open with Charlotte Daly's I'm Going To, in two parts. The Bean and the Stone follows, then Mayne Reid's adventure with dusky wolves. David Ker's sailor cat, a piece on the lion, and Livingstone's own lion adventure come next. Stories of Indian Spring and other tales fill the book. Pupils read for skill and for facts at once.
newton-forster:
Captain Frederick Marryat wrote Newton Forster, or The Merchant Service, a sea novel shown here in a Dent edition from London. Little, Brown in Boston shared the printing. The sampled copy gives a bare contents list of numbered chapters, with no heads to guide the reader.

The record's own summary fills the gap: young Newton Forster is pressed into the navy against his will. He suffers prison in France and shipwreck in the West Indies. At last he wins a post on an East India Company ship bound for Asia. Murder, press gangs, pirates, and romance crowd his path. Marryat knew that sea life from his own service.
no-surrender:
G. A. Henty subtitled No Surrender! as a tale of the rising in La Vendée, published in 1900. That rising set French peasants against the French Republic in revolution days. Chapter one opens with a French lugger, and the beginning of troubles follows. Cathelineau's scouts get their own chapter.

The record's summary names Leigh Stansfield, a young English lad drawn into the fight. He raises a band of boy scouts to serve the Vendéan army. Chapters cover the capture of Saumur, the attack on Nantes, and a stand at Le Mans. Leigh, per the summary, rescues his sister from the guillotine. In disguise, grave risk, and home close the tale.
note-book-of-an-english-opium-eater:
Thomas De Quincey filled his Note Book of an English Opium-Eater with essays on mixed subjects. Three Memorable Murders opens the contents, then the Bible's ties to human science. A literary history of the eighteenth century and Sophocles' Antigone follow. Milton against Southey and Landor gets a piece of its own.

Other essays treat the falsification of English history, suicide, and superficial knowledge. English dictionaries, Dryden's hexastich, and Pope's retort upon Addison close the list. The murders piece, dated 1854, calls itself a sequel to Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts. De Quincey jokes that gloomy readers who hate gaiety will not follow him.
notes-of-a-twenty-five-years-service-in-:
John McLean published volume one of his Notes of a Twenty-Five Years' Service in the Hudson's Bay Territory in London in 1849. Richard Bentley issued the two volume work. McLean says he first wrote the notes to while away lonely, wearisome hours. That is the lot, he adds, of the Indian trader.

Friends also wished to hear his adventures, he admits in his preface. His stronger defence is that the territory stays little known. No faithful picture, he says, has shown the Company's servants, the Indian traders, as they live. The degradation and misery of many Indian tribes, or remnants of tribes, also stay unknown. His notes aim to supply both.
nuttie-s-father:
Charlotte M. Yonge published Nuttie's Father in 1885, per the heading of this copy. Its contents open at St Ambrose's choir. Monks Horton follows, then heir hunting and a chapter called A Name. Suspense and the water-soldier come next in the list. That Man and The Father keep the title's puzzle in view.

New plumes, Bridgefield Egremont, and lawn tennis appear in later chapters listed here. The father of Nuttie is clearly the book's hidden centre, named in a chapter of his own. Yonge wrote family tales where duty, money, and secrets cross. A choir, an heir hunt, and a missing father promise all three in this one.
old-rose-and-silver:
Myrtle Reed wrote the romantic novel Old Rose and Silver. Music in the book comes from Wilson Smith's Entreaty. Grant Weber arranged that piece for piano, still unpublished. The contents open with a falling star and a welcome home. A violin voice and the Crosby twins follow.

Later chapters name a light on the altar. Father and son, white gloves, and penance appear in titles. Isabel arrives partway through the unfolding story. Reed writes in a tender, musical, sentimental style. Love, loss, and faith seem central to the tale. The book suits readers of gentle early romances.
on-the-frontier:
Bret Harte gathered these western stories in one volume. The contents open at the Mission of San Carmel. Other tales name a Blue Grass Penelope and Lone Star Mountain. The first story begins on August 10, 1838. Fog creeps over the dull California coast near Monterey.

Harte paints rounded hills, wild oats, and a glittering sea. A trading vessel gleams last before the fog closes in. Harte made the mining camp and frontier famous in fiction. His tales mix pathos, irony, and local color. They remain classics of the American West. A lone whaling ship or rare trader drifts past that shore. The far tower bell is lost in the strong sea winds.
opera-stories-from-wagner:
Florence Akin retold Richard Wagner's operas as stories in a 1915 book meant to bring the great music dramas within reach of ordinary readers. Her verses come from Oliver Huckel's English translations of the four Ring operas, printed with the publisher's permission, and the tales follow the operas in order.

The contents open with The Rhine-Gold: the happy Rhine-daughters, Alberich's theft of the gold, the wishing-cap, and a curse that hangs over everything after. A castle rises on the Rhine and the gods take their beautiful Valhalla. The Walküre follows, with the valiant Siegmund and his matchless sword. Told as continuous stories, the myths of gods, heroes, and cursed gold read like a saga.
other-tales-and-sketches-from-the-dolive:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Other Tales and Sketches collects three pieces left among his shorter writings: My Visit to Niagara, The Antique Ring, and Graves and Goblins. The Niagara sketch, which opens the set, is a small masterpiece of anti-climax. Hawthorne confesses he had delayed the visit for years, hoarding the anticipated wonder, and trembled with dread as the stagecoach neared the falls and he listened for their roar.

Then, at the moment of arrival, his enthusiasm fell into a deathlike slumber. He alighted with perfect composure, handed his cloak to the waiter, and asked not the way to the cataract but the dinner hour. The sketch anatomizes a familiar perversity of the mind — feeling nothing before the sublime — with Hawthorne's gentlest irony.
our-world-or-the-slaveholder-s-daughter:
F. Colburn Adams published Our World; Or, the Slaveholder's Daughter in 1855, in the flood of anti-slavery fiction that followed Uncle Tom's Cabin. His preface expects charges of misrepresenting Southern society and answers them in advance: read and digest, he tells slavery's champions, and you will find truth stranger than fiction. The book aims to picture Southern society in all its aspects.

The contents move through Marston's plantation by night and day. Unexpected confessions and a marooning party appear. So do pleasant dealings with human property. At last come two chapters of horror: They Are Going to Be Sold. And Let Us Follow Poor Human Nature to the Man Shambles. Adams lays every moral, social, and political evil he depicts directly at slavery's door.
paul-kelver: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Paul Kelver, Jerome K. Jerome's contents pages, with no chapter text visible. The contents are written as a pilgrim's progress for a boy named Paul, who arrives in a strange land. He meets the Man in Grey and the Man with the Ugly Mouth, and is shipwrecked and cast into deep waters. A prologue and two books are listed, the second opening on the desert island to which Paul drifted.
percy-bysshe-shelley-as-a-philosopher-an: The sample hosted here shows only the front matter of Percy Bysshe Shelley as a Philosopher and Reformer, the title page, copyright page, and the start of a dedication. No essay text is visible. The title page names Charles Sotheran and the New York publisher Charles P. Somerby, with copyright entered in 1876. It promises an original sonnet by Charles W. Frederickson, a portrait of Shelley, and a view of his tomb, and takes its motto from Shelley in 1822: let us see the truth, whatever that may be.
personal-recollections-of-pardee-butler:
Personal Recollections of Pardee Butler appeared at Cincinnati in 1889, from the Standard Publishing Company. Butler was a preacher of the Disciples of Christ whose recollections his daughter, Mrs. Rosetta B. Hastings, gathered and supplemented. Her preface admits she has not attempted a complete biography, since her father said little about his early years and kept no journal.

He had even destroyed most of his old letters, so she drew on relatives and friends. Elders John Boggs and J. B. McCleery added chapters from their own knowledge. The result is a daughter's tribute to a frontier preacher's earnest devotion to duty.
personality-plus-some-experiences-of-emm: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Personality Plus, the title page, contents, and list of illustrations, with no story text visible. The title page names Edna Ferber and promises some experiences of Emma McChesney and her son, Jock, with fifteen illustrations by James Montgomery Flagg. Frederick A. Stokes published the book in New York in 1914, and the contents list five pieces, from Making Good with Mother to The Self-Starter.
peter-s-mother:
Mrs. Henry de la Pasture wrote a special preface to the 1906 edition of Peter's Mother, addressed to her American readers. Wiseacres had warned her that her novels treat too narrow and circumscribed a life for Americans. She answers that a sincere portrait of a typical Englishwoman may attract them precisely by its strangeness.

Her heroine, Lady Mary Crewys, stands for hundreds of Englishwomen living guarded, isolated lives. Many, she notes, diffuse content and kindness while taking it for granted that their own wishes are of no account. The novel studies such a mother, and the son for whom she has surrendered herself.
phil-the-fiddler:
Horatio Alger's preface to Phil, the Fiddler, dated New York, April 1872, opens a window on New York's street children. The young Italian musicians who wander with harps, violins, and tambourines, he says, keep their foreign look and learn little English. Worse, speculators buy them from their parents in Italy and treat them inhumanly; one Italian editor calls them the white slaves of New York.

Alger got his facts from the superintendent of the Italian school at Five Points and from that editor's articles. His story of Phil, a fiddler boy, was meant to win sympathy and reform for the children it describes.
philosophical-letters-of-friedrich-schil:
Schiller's Philosophical Letters open with prefatory remarks on how reason grows. The reason, like the heart, passes through epochs and transitions, but men have rarely portrayed them.
