Degeneracy in morals, the remarks argue, roots in a one-sided philosophy, while an enlightened understanding ennobles the feelings: the heart must be formed by the head.

The contents promise the Theosophy of Julius and an essay on the connection between the animal and spiritual nature in man. Friends who reached the same convictions by different roads present these letters as a record of awakening reason, shoals and all.
phineas-finn-the-irish-member: A hosted sample showing only the front matter of Phineas Finn, the title page, publication note, and contents, with no chapter text visible. A note records that Anthony Trollope's novel first ran in St. Paul's Magazine from 1867 and appeared in book form in 1869. The contents follow the young Irish member from proposing to stand for Loughshane to taking his seat, meeting Lady Laura Standish and Violet Effingham, debating the ballot, and making his first speech.
plunkitt-of-tammany-hall-a-series-of-ver:
George Washington Plunkitt, a New York Tammany Hall leader and former state senator, gives his plain talks on practical politics in Plunkitt of Tammany Hall. William L Riordon recorded the talks, delivered from Plunkitt's rostrum, the county courthouse bootblack stand. Chapter titles in the contents run from Honest Graft and Dishonest Graft to How to Become a Statesman.

Across twenty-three short chapters, Plunkitt explains patronage, party loyalty, district holding, reformers, and the use of money in politics in his own blunt voice. He had held four public offices in one year, the preface notes. The book remains a rare inside account of machine politics by a proud practitioner.
poems-of-cheer:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox published Poems of Cheer in a London edition from Gay and Hancock in 1914. She used the front pages to warn British readers that any other firm's edition of her poems was pirated. The volume, she explains, contains the poems earlier issued as Poems of Life. Minus a handful that appear in her other books, plus a few new verses added for this collection.

Wilcox was America's most popular poet of optimism, and cheer is the program here: short, rhymed, quotable poems meant to lift ordinary readers through grief, work, and disappointment. The opening poem pictures the poet stepping across a border into the wonder-world of art, where mountain peaks stand near to God. Her direct, encouraging voice, scorned by critics and loved by millions, is on full display in this authorized London printing.
poems-of-power:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox explained the title of Poems of Power in a note at the front. The final word means the divine power inside every human being, whose recognition is the secret of all success and happiness. First published in 1903, the London edition from Gay and Hancock was reprinted again and again. Sixteen times by 1918, a measure of how hungry readers were for her gospel of self-command.

Contents mix consolation and command: the Queen's Last Ride, the Meeting of the Centuries, Grief, Illusion, and Assertion. The poems teach her familiar lessons, that thought shapes fate, that sorrow can be mastered, that the will is a real force. Wilcox stood at the head of the New Thought movement's popular wing, and Poems of Power is her doctrine in verse. The book her admirers kept by the bed and quoted in letters of sympathy.
poker:
Zora Neale Hurston wrote Poker!, a one-act play copyrighted in 1931 and preserved in a manuscript carrying penciled edits, possibly in her own hand. The scene is a shabby front room in a Harlem shotgun house: a battered piano, gaudy calendars, kerosene lamps. A card table where Tush Hawg riffles the deck like an expert and calls Nunkie away from the piano to take a hand he has been bragging about.

Characters carry folk names, Too-Sweet, Peckerwood, Black Baby, Sack Daddy, and Aunt Dilsey, and the talk is the show. Boasting, teasing, and verbal dueling in Black vernacular that Hurston collected as a trained folklorist. The play stayed unpublished in her lifetime, like much of her theater work. Read now, it is a small, perfect specimen of Hurston turning the speech of her people into literature without sanding off its shine.
preliminary-report-of-the-commission-app:
The University of Pennsylvania appointed this commission, at the request of the late Henry Seybert, to investigate modern spiritualism, and its preliminary report, with a foreword by H. H. Furness Jr., appeared in editions of 1887 and 1920. Seybert had left money for exactly this test, and the commissioners, busy men donating fragments of time, present their first findings frankly as fragmentary. They ask to be continued, since belief in spiritualism is not decreasing and now claims rank among the denominations.

Their letter to the trustees sets the tone: earnest, procedural, and unimpressed. The Seybert Commission sat through séances, examined mediums, and found the phenomena wanting, a verdict that made the report famous in the long war between science and the séance room. As a document it preserves the moment a great university formally cross-examined the spirits, and printed what the spirits failed to answer.
prince-henry-the-navigator-the-hero-of-p:
Prince Henry of Portugal fills this volume of the Heroes of the Nations series under the title Hero of Portugal and of Modern Discovery, 1394 to 1460. The series list at the front shows the company he keeps: Nelson, Gustavus Adolphus, Pericles. Theodoric, Sidney, Julius Caesar, Wyclif, Napoleon, and Henry of Navarre, each written for the general reader. Henry's claim on the shelf is the strangest, since he never sailed on the voyages he made possible.

From Sagres his school of pilots, cartographers, and captains pushed the African coast open cape by cape, reaching Madeira, the Azores. Sierra Leone within his lifetime and preparing the sea road to India that da Gama sailed a generation after his death. The series biography tells that story as national epic. Henry remains its presiding genius: the prince who stayed home and moved the world.
princess-polly-s-gay-winter:
Amy Brooks wrote a storybook for children about Rose Atherton and her friends at Avondale, where Uncle John keeps a fine house called The Cliffs above the sea. Rose looks back on a happy summer at the shore and hears that merry times are promised for the winter ahead.

Chapters move through school days, a breath of the sea, Aunt Judith's party, a holiday party, and a promise made by Uncle John. Gwen and Gyp share in the fun and small troubles. Young readers get gentle lessons in kindness and cheer told through parties, calls, and play.
quiet-talks-on-prayer:
Quiet Talks on Prayer, by S. D. Gordon, copyrighted in 1904 by Fleming H. Revell Company, sets out the meaning and mission of prayer, the hindrances to it, how to pray, and Jesus' own habits of prayer. Its first part calls prayer the greatest outlet of power and the deciding factor in a spirit conflict.

The hindrances section asks why results fail or are delayed, and the practical part treats method, the listening side of prayer, and God's will. The book closes with a sketch of Jesus at prayer, from dissolving views and deepening shadows to a composite picture under the olive trees.
quotations-from-the-pg-collected-works-o: Quotations from the Collected Works of Gilbert Parker is a Widger's Quotations volume drawn from the Project Gutenberg edition of Parker's collected novels. The pages shown hold David Widger's editor's note and the first contents line, Pierre. Widger invites readers who know the novels to check for their favorite passages. He invites them to send additions. He also explains how to trace any extract back to its full context. The context stands in the source file.
quotes-and-images-from-the-confessions-o:
Quotes and Images from Harry Lorrequer draws on The Confessions of Harry Lorrequer. The 1839 Dublin novel is generally credited to Charles James Lever (1806-1872). Its title page bore no author's name. David Widger's headnote explains that the first edition's pages were too stained and brittle to scan. The book was typed out by hand for its electronic edition.

Harry was a young officer whose regiment was posted in Ireland in the early 1800s. The extracts keep his mess-room humor. A crowd is a mob, one line runs, even if composed of bishops, and men are found hating each other for the love of God.
quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of-char: Quotes and Images from Charles Dudley Warner is shown here by the contents of Warner's writings, the essay books from which David Widger drew his extracts. The list runs from Summer in a Garden to Being a Boy. Backlog Studies, Baddeck, and In the Wilderness stand between. On Horseback and Their Pilgrimage follow. Essays on modern fiction, literary copyright, education, and American life appear. A second set includes Night in the Tuileries. It includes Pursuit of Happiness too.
quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of-gilb:
Quotes and Images from the Works of Gilbert Parker is prepared by David Widger. It sets the Canadian novelist's sentences in alphabetical order. Each extract runs a line or two. They come from his tales of the north and of French Canada.

A human life, one entry runs, he held to be a trifle in the big sum of time, and a heart-break is the salvation of that kind. A man may be forgiven for a sin, but the effect remains. Parker gives us a man you could bank on, a cloak of words to cover the real thought, and the agony of thinking about the things we are never going to do.
raabe-alte-nester:
Returning home after long years away tests Raabe's characters in Alte Nester, given here in German. Old Nests follows men and women circling back to family and the places that shaped them. Time has changed everything and nothing, which is the novel's tender problem.

Old friendships revive, old wounds reopen, and the nests of the title prove both shelter and trap. Raabe writes with mature wisdom and gentle irony, never mocking the homesickness he portrays. Reconciliation comes slowly, where it comes at all. The novel satisfies deeply as a story about roots and what they cost. German readers rank it high among his later works, and its warmth explains why.
raftmates-a-story-of-the-great-river: Raftmates, a story of the great river by Kirk Munroe, was published by Harper and Brothers in 1902, with an 1893 copyright. Only the title page and contents are shown. The chapters promise a boys' river voyage. The Raft opens the list. Winn Assumes a Responsibility follows. Billy Brackett Starts Down the River comes next. A gang of river-traders appears. So does the disappearance of the raft. A night alone on the island follows. The trappers are trapped. Cap'n Cod, with Sabella and the Whatnot, closes this part.
reading-made-easy-for-foreigners-third-r:
John L. Hülshof, a teacher of modern languages in the public schools of New York City, wrote this third reader for learners new to English. The book was copyrighted in 1909 by Hinds, Noble and Eldredge of New York. A note to the teacher stands at the front, before the graded lessons begin.

Lesson titles mix civic themes with short talks on daily life and character. Pupils read about Flag Day, the national flag, and the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor. Other lessons treat pure air, coffee, trifles, tact, and good behavior. Later pieces turn to George Washington, Rosa Bonheur, Alexander and the Robber, the American Indian, and the first steamboat.
rebel-raider:
H. Beam Piper wrote this Civil War tale for True: The Man's Magazine, where it appeared in December 1950. The scene is the Ratcliffe home in Fairfax County, Virginia, near midnight on January 2, 1863. General J. E. B. Stuart is the guest of honor at a party that is breaking up.

Stuart had raided up from Culpeper with strong cavalry, shooting up outposts and burning stores of forage over Christmas. Before riding back, he tells his hostess Laura Ratcliffe that he will not desert the loyal people there. Captain Mosby will stay behind with a few men to look after them. The tale follows that choice and the raider left in enemy-held ground.
recreations-in-astronomy-with-directions:
Henry White Warren, D.D., wrote this guide to the heavens for general readers, with eighty-three pictures and star maps. Its full title promises directions for hands-on trials and work with a telescope. A front plate notes the stars of Orion and Taurus, their colors, and the Crab Nebula.

Warren's preface says astronomy moves at the double-quick while other sciences merely advance. Since Copernicus settled its first rules four hundred years before, it has never had to beat a retreat. New finds, not old errors, force its books to be rewritten. Stars once read as fixed points of light are now studied in depth.
red-masquerade-being-the-story-of-the-lo:
Louis Joseph Vance published this tale of the Lone Wolf's daughter in 1921, after a film of the same name in the autumn of 1919. His apology at the front admits the book derives, quite brazenly, from his own invention for the screen. He took, he says, as many liberties with the film version as its director took with his story.

The book is dedicated to J. Parker Read, Jr., who produced that film, and Vance signs his note at Westport on December 31, 1920. A front picture shows Prince Victor asking, with pain, whether he must tell all. Doubleday, Page and the Pictorial Review, where the tale ran as a serial, share his thanks.
reminiscences-of-a-pioneer:
Colonel William Thompson, editor of the Alturas Plaindealer, published his pioneer memories at San Francisco in 1912. His contents start with a farewell to the old southern home and a first winter in the Willamette Valley. An Indian outbreak of 1855 follows, with tales of Canyon City and his first newspaper venture.

The Modoc wars fill the middle chapters: a history of the Modoc Indians, the Ben Wright massacre, a treaty, and battles in the Lava Beds. The Peace Commission's work and the trailing of fugitives come next. Later chapters cover the Great Bannock War, a Snake uprising in eastern Oregon, the reign of the vigilantes, and the Lookout lynching.
reveries-of-a-schoolmaster:
Francis B. Pearson, state superintendent of public instruction for Ohio, muses on his trade in this book, copyrighted by Scribner in 1917. Pearson had also written The Evolution of the Teacher and The Vitalized School. His twenty-seven chapters bear short, teasing names rather than plain school topics.

In Medias Res and Retrospect open the set, followed by Brown, Psychological, and Balking. Lanterns, Complete Living, and My Speech stand beside a chapter plainly named School-Teaching. Beefsteak, Hoeing Potatoes, Picnics, and Rabbit Pedagogy keep the tone homely and wry. Story-Telling, Grandmother, and Perspective close a schoolman's daydreams on freedom, behavior, and the point of view.
ritchie-s-fabulae-faciles-a-first-latin-:
John Copeland Kirtland, Jr., professor of Latin at the Phillips Exeter Academy, edited this first Latin reader from Ritchie's Fabulae Faciles, with notes and a vocabulary. He dedicates his small share of the book to Professor Joseph Hetherington McDaniels, his teacher and friend. Lists at the front place the myths in English literature and in art.

Four story groups form the reader: Perseus, Hercules, the Argonauts, and Ulysses. Pictures show Danae and Perseus shut in the ark, Hercules with Nessus and Dejanira, and Ulysses with Circe. The opening list names later retellings a pupil may know, from Hawthorne's Wonder-Book and Kingsley's Heroes to William Morris's Earthly Paradise.
robert-falconer:
George MacDonald tells the story of Robert Falconer from the boy's own boyhood, in a novel whose Scots speech is aided by a glossary. The glossary, a note explains, was compiled for this electronic text and does not belong to the original work. MacDonald dedicates the book to the memory of Alexander John Scott, who stands highest in the oratory of his memory.

Part one, His Boyhood, opens with a recollection. Robert, a schoolboy of fourteen, had thought he had never seen his father. A vision dawns on him: a Sunday afternoon reading The Pilgrim's Progress to his grandmother, a tap at the door, and a tall, haggard man in a shabby black coat standing there.
robur-der-sieger:
Julius Verne's Robur tale appears here in German as Robur der Sieger, from the Bibliographische Anstalt Adolph Schumann at Leipzig. A note adds that other translations of Robur-le-Conquérant appeared as Robur der Eroberer. Chapter one opens, as in the French tale, with two pistol shots and an innocent cow struck near Niagara.

The duelists had quarrelled over a trumpet tune heard from the sky between Lakes Ontario and Erie the night before. The German text goes on where its scene ends: a strange appearance had crossed America, then Europe a day later, then Asia, puzzling every head for a month. No balloon could explain it, and men wondered if an angel's trumpet had sounded.
roden-s-corner:
Henry Seton Merriman published this novel in 1913, under a verse from Omar Khayyam on destiny playing with men as pieces on a chequer-board. Its contents open In St. Jacob Straat, a Dutch street name that sets the scene abroad. Beginning at Home and A New Disciple follow.

Out of Egypt, On the Dunes, and In the Oude Weg keep the Dutch ground in view. Official and The Seamy Side darken the middle of the list. A Shadow from the Past, Deeper Water, and Unsound mark the fall toward crisis. The Making of a Man and Plain Speaking close the chapters shown, in a tale of work, money, and character tested in a foreign city.
rosamond-or-the-youthful-error-a-tale-of:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes, author of Tempest and Sunshine and Lena Rivers, tells this tale of Riverside under the title Rosamond, or The Youthful Error. Its contents open with The Owner of Riverside, then name the heroine herself: Rosamond Leyton. Ben's Visit and Rosamond's Education follow.

Brother and Sister and Marie Porter fill the middle chapters shown. Making Love heads the seventh, as the youthful error of the subtitle takes shape. Other stories stand with the tale in the volume, as its title promises, though their names fall beyond the contents shown. Riverside, its owner, and its people fill the tale's opening world.
rose-o-the-river: Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote Rose O' the River, with pictures by George Wright, first issued in September 1905. The contents list fourteen chapters, opening with The Pine and the Rose and Old Kennebec, then The Edgewood Drive and The Game of Jackstraws. Later titles include Hearts and Other Hearts, The Little House, The Garden of Eden, The Serpent, The Turquoise Ring, and The Dream Room. Four pictures are listed, with Rose O' the River as the front piece.
rujub-the-juggler:
G. A. Henty wrote Rujub, the Juggler, which the publishers present as chiefly a history tale for young and old. Its subject is the Sepoy Mutiny in India during the years 1857 to 1859, under Lord Canning's rule. The publishers trace the rising to signs such as cakes of flour and water passed among the people and placards at Delhi against British rule. A new Enfield rifle, with greased cartridges said to be smeared with pig's fat, lit the fuse among Sepoy soldiers serving the Queen.

Their account runs through the first outbreak at Meerut, the march on Delhi, the surrender at Cawnpore and the killing that followed, and the siege of Lucknow. Europeans at Lucknow held out for about three months and were near giving up when General Havelock's march relieved them. Sir Colin Campbell followed, and British rule was restored step by step.
running-water: A. E. W. Mason, author of The Four Feathers, wrote Running Water, dated 1907. The contents list nineteen chapters, opening with Mrs. Thesiger in her home, one of Strood's successors, and The Finding of John Lattery. Later titles include Mr. Jarvice, Michel Revailloud Expounds His Philosophy, The Pavillon de Lognan, and The Aiguille d'Argentiere. The second half turns to Sylvia parting from her mother, Sylvia meeting her father, The House of the Running Water, Chayne Returns, and The Shadow in the Room.
said-the-observer: Louis J. Stellmann wrote Said the Observer, with pictures by J. P. Burnham and V. C. Forsythe, issued at San Francisco in 1903. A front picture is captioned The Telephone Face. Stellmann gives the book to his mother on her fiftieth birthday, in a long verse dedication. The poem weighs half a century of gladness and half a century of tears, lost in the silence of past years.
select-poems-of-sidney-lanier: Morgan Callaway edited a choice of poems by Sidney Lanier for this volume. The pages at hand carry only the publisher's header for the electronic edition, with the title, Lanier's name, and Callaway's role as editor. A note adds that the file was typed twice by hand and checked by machine for accuracy. No poem text or contents list appears in these opening pages, so which of Lanier's poems Callaway chose cannot be stated from what is shown here.
self-development-and-the-way-to-power:
L. W. Rogers published this short book in 1922, priced at twenty-five cents. Rogers holds that joy is man's natural state and pain the fruit of ignorance. A motto states the choice plainly: men may be slaves of nature who suffer, or glad masters of her laws.

Rogers argues that wisdom ends suffering by showing why loss, betrayal, and poverty strike without clear cause. Growth, in his view, is a forced march of the spirit toward light. Readers seeking strength of mind meet a plain-spoken call to study life's hidden laws and rule the self by knowledge rather than fear.
set-in-silver:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson published this motoring novel with Doubleday, Page in 1913, from a 1909 copyright. They dedicate the tale to a great man and great motorist, and to a tour in the land he loves. England itself, praised in a famed verse passage, gives the book its title.

Letters carry the tale, opening with Audrie Brendon writing to her mother from Versailles. A car tour through England forms the route, with love and mishap along the roads. The Williamsons blend travel charm with courtship, in the light manner that made their motor tales popular on both sides of the Atlantic.
sidney-lanier: Edwin Mims wrote this biography of the poet Sidney Lanier. The pages at hand carry only the publisher's header for the electronic edition. That header gives the title and Mims's name. It also notes care in preparing the file. No chapter text appears here. No contents list or life detail is shown. Lanier's story cannot be told from the header alone. Mims's judgment of the verse and music must wait for pages beyond these.
sima-qian-memoires-historiques-chavannes:
The first tome of Édouard Chavannes's French Shiji appeared in 1895, the start of a ten-year labor. Sima Qian wrote the Records of the Grand Historian around 91 BCE. Chavannes opens with chapters one through four, the deep past of China as the Han court knew it.

Here are the Five Emperors of legend, then the Xia, Shang, and Zhou houses in their annals. Chavannes adds long notes that test the tales against other early texts. His French version became the standard Western door into the Shiji. This tome lays the mythic base on which the whole history stands.
simon-called-peter:
Robert Keable published this novel in 1921 and dedicated it to Julie, a woman he calls perhaps invented yet deathless. A note to the reader opens on the glamour of war, that strong lure no sorrow seems to kill. Each new age forgets, Keable warns, and talks of heroism at hell's mouth.

The war of 1914-1918 came near to war's final condemnation, Keable argues. Men died bravely to end war itself, and heard the guns stop on November 11, 1918, hoping that end had come. Keable fears betrayal of that hope. His tale of a chaplain tests faith against war's wreckage.
simon-the-jester:
William J. Locke wrote this novel around a narrator who opens by hunting the most godforsaken spot in England. His friend Renniker, a clubman who knows all things, names Murglebed-on-Sea, a fashionable resort in villainous November. The narrator pleads that his question is serious, and Renniker holds his ground.

The narrator sends his man Rogers ahead to inspect the place and report. Rogers goes light-hearted, thinking his master mad, and returns much altered. Locke sets a tale of a jesting man facing a grave fate in a dreary seaside town, mixing wit with an ache that deepens as Simon's story unfolds.
skyrider: B. M. Bower wrote Skyrider, dated 1919, with a front picture by Anton Otto Fischer, printed at Boston by Little, Brown, and Company. The contents open with a poet without honor, one fight, two quarrels, and a riddle. Johnny then rides to Sinkhole, and later heads speak of salvage, a midnight ride, and signs that no one can read. A hawk-like thing that settles over the herd marks the early chapters.
some-old-time-beauties-after-portraits-b: Thomson Willing wrote the notes for Some Old Time Beauties, after portraits by the English masters, printed at Boston by Joseph Knight Company in the year MDCCCXCV, that is, 1895. The contents lead with Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, and Mary, the Honorable Mrs. Graham, both from portraits by Thomas Gainsborough. Emma, Lady Hamilton, by George Romney, and Mrs. Sheridan, by Sir Joshua Reynolds, come next, with Marguerite, Countess Blessington, by Sir Thomas Lawrence.
st-martin-s-summer: Rafael Sabatini wrote St. Martin's Summer, first published in 1921, though one line in the front matter gives 1909. The contents open with the Seneschal of Dauphiny and Monsieur de Garnache. Heads then name the dowager's compliance and the chateau de Condillac. Monsieur de Garnache loses his temper in one chapter and keeps it in the next, and the opening and closing of a trap frame the seneschal's advice, a recruit, and Valerie's gaoler.
star-hunter:
Andre Norton sets Star Hunter on the world Nahuatl. Ace Books held its 1961 copyright. Nahuatl's larger moon chases a smaller, greenish globe. The stars make a speckled pattern in the clear sky. They look like scales of a huge serpent. That serpent coils round a black bowl. Ras Hume pauses on the top terrace of the Pleasure House. Scented spike-flowers edge that terrace. He asks himself why he thinks of serpents.

He knows the reason well. Man's age-old hatred came with him to the far stars. Evil takes a serpent's shape in that hatred. Wass is the serpent on Nahuatl. A dozen other worlds know Wass as well. A night wind stirs the off-world leaves on the terrace. Those leaves fake a jungle's mystery there. A voice from thin air calls Hume's name. A shaft of bright light then strikes through the dark.
steve-yeager:
Steve Yeager, a western novel by William MacLeod Raine, carries a 1915 copyright and a New York printing by Grosset and Dunlap. The contents promise a fast chain of trouble. Steve makes a mistake and meets Chad Harrison. He rides into the desert and follows a night trail. He faces cave men, a prisoner, and a stage set for tragedy.

Other chapters bring in Gabriel Pasquale and Pedro Cabenza, a night visit, a plot, and a trap, with Ruth shown in the frontispiece. Raine builds the story from short, punchy episodes in open country, where loyalties shift and each wrong move pushes Yeager nearer the end of his trail.
stifter-der-nachsommer:
Under the guidance of a wise older man at the country estate of Asperhof, a young visitor grows into a life of art, nature, and order. Stifter's Der Nachsommer, given here in German, follows that slow education across a long, serene novel. Its title means Indian summer, the season of ripe, golden calm.

Gardens, paintings, geology, and measured conversation fill the days at Asperhof. Nothing hurries; meaning gathers through patient attention to beautiful and useful things. Judges call it the most serene novel in German literature, and the phrase fits. Demanding in its slowness, the book is deeply rewarding to readers who surrender to it. It stands as the supreme statement of Stifter's gentle law of life.
stories-from-the-trenches-humorous-and-l:
Carleton B. Case gathered Stories from the Trenches from what he calls authentic sources. The subtitle promises humorous and lively doings of our boys over there. Shrewesbury Publishing Company of Chicago copyrighted the book in 1918. It collects jokes, yarns, and short reports from American soldiers in the Great War.

The contents open with The Man Who Came Back, move through Franco-Yanko Romances and Trench Superstitions, and follow In the Trail of the Hun. A flying piece tells of the ace Lufbery bagging his thirteenth machine. The tone stays light on purpose, giving home readers the funny side of trench life rather than its horrors.
summer:
Edith Wharton's Summer, dated 1917, is a short novel of a New England village. It opens at North Dormer, a high, open place of one street. A girl comes out of lawyer Royall's house. It is the start of a June afternoon. She stands on the doorstep.

Silver sunshine falls on roofs, pastures, and larchwoods, and a little wind shakes the spruces by the Hatchard gate. It catches the straw hat of a passing young man. He is a stranger in city clothes. The wind spins the hat into the duck pond. The girl watches him laugh as he fishes it out. That meeting, in the village where the girl has felt trapped and watched over, sets the novel's summer of longing and risk in motion.
t-mann-tonio-kroger:
A young writer torn between the solid bourgeois world and the artist's bohemia carries Mann's novella Tonio Kroeger, given here in German. Tonio loves the blond, ordinary, happy people he can never quite join. His success as an author only sharpens the exile he feels at every homecoming.

North against south, discipline against passion: the story arranges Tonio's whole life along those poles. A trip back to his Baltic hometown and on to Denmark frames his confession of faith in ordinary life. Mann called Tonio his most autobiographical figure, and artists have recognized themselves in him ever since. The essential Mann novella reads here in its original German. Few short works state his lifelong theme so cleanly.
tales-of-a-traveller:
Washington Irving's Tales of a Traveller is built in four parts. The first part is Strange Stories by a Nervous Gentleman. It gathers tales told at a hunting dinner. They include the adventure of the German student. They include a mysterious picture and a mysterious stranger. They include the story of the young Italian.

Part two turns to Buckthorne and his friends, with a literary life, a literary dinner, the club of queer fellows, and the poor devil author. Part three follows the Italian banditti through the inn at Terracina and the stories of a bandit chieftain and a young robber. Part four is The Money Diggers. It gives Hell Gate and Kidd the pirate. It gives The Devil and Tom Walker too. That is Irving's famous bargain tale. It treats a miser, a swamp, and the devil's gold in colonial New England.
tales-of-daring-and-danger:
G. A. Henty wrote Tales of Daring and Danger, issued in London by Blackie and Son in 1890 with pictures throughout. Five tales are listed, among them Bears and Dacoits, The Paternosters, A Pipe of Mystery, White-Faced Dick, and A Brush with the Chinese.

Henty was known for bold adventure tales for young readers, and the titles here promise wild beasts, outlaws, and fights in far-off lands. The opening tale, Bears and Dacoits, points to India, where dacoits were armed robbers. Readers who like fast action and brave deeds in strange places will find the book aimed squarely at them.
tanakh-jps-1917-esther:
Esther is a short narrative book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation of the Holy Scriptures. The tale is set at the Persian court, in the reign of Ahasuerus, whose rule ran from India to Ethiopia.

Chapter one shows the king on his throne at Shushan, feasting his princes for a full half year in great pomp. Rich hangings, gold cups, and wine poured with a free hand fill the palace court. Queen Vashti also holds a feast of her own. Readers enter a court tale of pride, banquets, and sudden turns, where a queen's fate and a people's fate will soon hang on chance and nerve.
ten-years-later: Alexandre Dumas wrote Ten Years Later. It forms part three of the Vicomte de Bragelonne in his D'Artagnan tales. A front note sorts out the set's split volumes. The note dates this part to 1660 and 1661. It gives chapters 76 to 140. It warns of a same-named text with chapters 1 to 104. That text overlaps parts of two other volumes. The note calls this a source of much mix-up among readers.
tennessee-s-partner:
Bret Harte's Tennessee's Partner appears here as Western Classics number three, with an opening essay by William Dallam Armes. A short quote sets the tone, calling both men fearless types of a rough, bold age.

Armes recalls how Marshall's gold find drew crowds from all lands to a California left with weak, strange rule. Mexican law still stood on paper while free and slave states fought over the new land's voice. Yet the mining camps, left to rule themselves, chose local heads and kept rough order. Readers then meet Harte's famed tale of two partners, loyalty, and a hanging, set in that raw gold camp world.
the-adventures-of-a-boy-reporter: Harry Steele Morrison wrote The Adventures of a Boy Reporter in 1900. Chapter heads trace Archie from country school first. A Hut Club and a circus visit come next. A trip to New York with Uncle Henry follows. Archie then flees home at night in secret. Harsh farm work comes after that. A night among ruins with tramps follows. He steals a ride and lands in a Bowery lodging house. Dish work in a Bowery restaurant comes next. A kind editor at a newspaper office then takes him in.
the-adventures-of-joel-pepper: Margaret Sidney wrote The Adventures of Joel Pepper. It is a tale for young readers. A front plate shows Joel in mid-cry. He has just spied the man who stole Polly's bread. Chapters listed start with Joel and the Snake. Deacon Brown's Nail Pile comes next. The Muffin Man and the Tramp follow. Circus Plans stands near the end. In the Little Brown House closes the list.
the-adventures-of-lightfoot-the-deer: Thornton W. Burgess wrote Lightfoot the Deer, with art by Harrison Cady, held under rights in 1921 and printed by Grosset and Dunlap of New York by arrangement with Little, Brown, and Company. Burgess gives the book to the deer of the Green Forest, in hope that it may aid the guarding of the innocent and helpless among wild things.
the-adventures-of-mr-mocker: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Mr. Mocker in 1914. Harrison Cady drew the plates. It is a Green Forest tale in twenty-five chapters. Heads track a lone traveler first. Unc' Billy Possum's vain search follows. Sammy Jay sits up all night next. He hopes to solve a voice riddle. Blacky the Crow's plan comes midway. A party given by Unc' Billy closes the book.
the-adventures-of-paddy-beaver: Little, Brown and Company printed The Adventures of Paddy Beaver at Boston and Toronto. Thornton W. Burgess wrote the tale, with rights held in 1917. Chapters listed open with Paddy the Beaver Begins Work. Paddy Plans a Pond comes next. Paddy Has Many Visitors follows. Sammy Jay then speaks his mind. Farmer Brown's boy grows curious after that. Peter Rabbit gets a ducking near the end.
the-adventures-of-paddy-the-beaver: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Paddy the Beaver, and this copy opens with Project Gutenberg front matter rather than the tale itself. The front pages point readers to an improved illustrated HTML edition filed as ebook 19092, then run through the standard Gutenberg notes on rights, reuse, and gifts before the title page begins.
the-amateur-poacher:
Richard Jefferies begins this book of country life with a boyhood memory: an old flintlock gun kept in a dark garret corner. A stuffed fox with a fine brush stood guard over it, grinning at any child bold enough to climb the stairs. The gun was forbidden, which made it all the more magnetic.

That first chapter, The First Gun, mixes fear and longing in equal parts. Shutter chinks let in thin light, loose stairs creak, and tales told by carters and old women feed a child's dread. Jefferies builds his later field lore on such early hunger for wild places, birds, and poaching craft learned close to home.
the-american-newspaper:
Charles Dudley Warner takes the American newspaper as his theme for an hour's talk. Everyone, he jokes, feels well informed on the press, and he has never met a person unable to edit a paper, though some cannot pay for one. He sets aside talk of the press's power and duty and asks for a deeper account instead.

Warner wants the paper read as a true product of its age, like public schooling, and asks what it does to the minds it feeds. A sharp, shallow, half-informed reader, quick and sure of himself, may be its clearest result. His own task, he says, is the humbler one of starting that inquiry.
the-american-spirit-in-literature-a-chro:
Bliss Perry's The American Spirit in Literature, issued in 1918 by Yale University Press as volume 34 of the Chronicles of America Series, traces the nation's writing from its first days. Chapters move from pioneers and early colonial work through the Revolution and the Knickerbocker group. Later heads treat the Transcendentalists, romance, poetry, and history, then Poe and Whitman.

Perry opens by calling the United States a land in constant change, marked by bodily and mental restlessness. His later chapters cover union and liberty in war years and the rise of a new nation. A short book list and an index close the volume, which aims to name the great voices who gave American life its shape in print.
the-american-union-speaker:
Entered for copyright in 1865 by John D. Philbrick in Massachusetts and printed at the Riverside Press in Cambridge, this speaker gathers pieces for recital and elocution practice. Its preface states a twofold aim: fresh selections fit for the spirit of the hour, and a choice set of standard pieces that time has already sealed.

About one hundred new extracts from more than fifty authors appear here for the first time in such a book. Most were stirred by the present national crisis. Sumner lays bare the roots of rebellion, and Douglass strips off its pretext. Everett paints its crime. Boutwell proclaims emancipation its remedy, and Banks blesses early reconstruction.
the-answer:
H. Beam Piper's short tale The Answer is noted as coming from Fantastic Universe Science Fiction of December 1959, with no sign found that its copyright was ever renewed. It opens as a screen door snaps and wakes Lee Richardson from a dream he fights to hold.

In the dream a slim woman with graying blonde hair plays with a small dachshund among new-fallen leaves on a lawn. His friend Alexis Pitov calls to him, and Richardson answers that he had fallen asleep. He is glad the picture stays with him as he wakes. Piper sets that tender scrap of memory at the head of a tale whose title promises a hard reply to come.
the-armies-of-labor-a-chronicle-of-the-o:
Samuel P. Orth wrote this chronicle of the organized wage-earner as volume 40 of the Chronicles of America Series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters move from a background and formative years through transition, amalgamation, and federation. Later heads treat the trade union, the railway brotherhoods, issues and warfare, the I. W. W., and labor in politics.

Orth opens with three signs of the era that starts in 1776: the Declaration of Independence, the steam engine, and Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations. The Declaration, he writes, birthed a nation whose millions of acres of free land would shift the balance of the world's trade. The engine and the book worked their own changes beside it.
the-art-of-the-story-teller:
Marie L. Shedlock's book on the story-teller's craft opens with a preface by another hand. Some day, that preface dreams, the science of teaching will match the science of medicine. Yet even then the art of teaching will stay the guide of wise teachers, since each new crop of children must still be led by artists who keep a child's direct sight.

The writer recalls hearing Shedlock tell stories in England some years ago. Her fine sense of worth in books and drama, her warm yet restrained readings, and her grasp of teaching all marked her as an artist. She was at home, the preface says, with the wit of Daudet, the folk wisdom of Grimm, and deeper world thought alike.
the-autobiography-of-a-slander:
Edna Lyall published her tale in a new Longmans edition in 1890, after earlier printings had reached tens of thousands of copies. A line from Sheridan warns readers not to trust each accusing tongue. The book is dedicated, pointedly, to all whom it may concern.

A slander speaks in the first person and dates its birth to September 2, 1886, in a dull country town called Muddleton. Tea-table talk gives it life. From that start, Lyall can trace how a false story grows, moves from house to house, and harms people who had little chance to answer it.
the-avenger:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published his thriller in 1908, with pictures by Alec Ball. Oppenheim is listed for earlier books such as The Master Mummer, A Maker of History, and The Great Secret. Chapter headings open with a mysterious visitor and a horror in a hansom cab.

Talk of a crime, a cloud over a suspect, and a telephone call follow in the contents. A reward of one thousand pounds is offered, a colonel's daughter enters, and a baroness steps in. Later headings name a box at the Alhambra, an outcast, news from the Cape, and a search of chambers, promising intrigue in London and beyond.
the-barrier:
Rex Beach set his novel on a last frontier, with pictures by Denman Fink. Chapter headings name Poleon Doret, whose hand is quicker than his tongue, and a soldier who finds an untrodden valley. A Burrell code, the magic of Ben Stark, and a knife follow.

Illustration captions name Necia, a girl who misses her father, and Poleon watching her with five years of waiting behind him. Later chapters promise a mystery unravelled and a knot tightened, John Gale's hour, and Runnion finding singing people. Love, codes of honour, and frontier conflict drive the tale toward a call named for mountain nymphs.
the-beacon-second-reader:
James H. Fassett's second reader was copyrighted in 1914 and published by Ginn and Company in Boston, New York, Chicago, and other cities. Contents mix rhymes, fairy tales, poems, and myths for young pupils. Early items include an old English rhyme about a ship and a Grimm tale of a wolf and seven young kids.

Further pages list Tom Thumb, Cinderella, and Rumpelstiltskin, along with poems by Phoebe Cary, Alice Cary, Tennyson, and Robert Louis Stevenson. A Greek myth of the golden touch, a German tale of a bell, and a Scottish tale of Bruce and the spider follow. Short pieces, named authors, and page numbers help teachers choose readings.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-13-1-paralip:
First Paralipomenon, also called First Chronicles, in Douay-Rheims translation, worked from the Latin Vulgate and later put through Bishop Richard Challoner's hands in 1749 to 1752. The older printings were a Douay Old Testament (1609, 1610) and a Rheims New Testament (1582). An introduction says these books were written after the books of Kings. They were probably shortened from ancient records of the days by Esdras or another sacred writer.

Chapter one gives a genealogy of the patriarchs down to Abraham. It then traces the posterity of Abraham and of Esau. Names, lines, and descent carry the history rather than battles or speeches. For readers, the lists anchor later stories in family lines reaching back to the earliest figures of Genesis.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-14-2-paralip:
Second Paralipomenon, also called Second Chronicles, in Douay-Rheims wording, Englished from the Latin Vulgate and revised under Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Rheims printed the New Testament in 1582; Douay printed the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610. Chapter one places Solomon with a great multitude at the high place of Gabaon.

There stood the tabernacle of the covenant made by Moses in the wilderness. A note recalls that David had brought the ark of God from Cariathiarim to a place he prepared. Worship at an old shrine, a king leading the people, and the ark's earlier journey open the book. Solomon's reign begins in public devotion rather than in war or building.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-26-ecclesias:
Ecclesiasticus, in Douay-Rheims wording, Englished from the Latin Vulgate and revised under Bishop Richard Challoner, 1749 to 1752. Rheims printed the New Testament in 1582; Douay printed the Old Testament in 1609 and 1610. An introduction says it was first written in Hebrew, then translated into Greek by another Jesus, the author's grandson. That grandson's prologue follows.

The prologue praises knowledge shown through the law, the prophets, and others who followed them. Israel is commended for doctrine and wisdom, he says, and readers in other lands should gain from it too. Family transmission matters here: a grandfather's Hebrew teaching carried into Greek by his own kin. Moral instruction for conduct fills the book that the prologue introduces.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-17-est:
Esther in King James translation, starts in the days of Ahasuerus, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces. In the third year of his reign he sits on his throne at Shushan the palace.

He makes a feast for princes and servants, showing the riches of his kingdom for one hundred and eighty days. A second feast follows for all people present at Shushan, great and small, for seven days in a palace garden court. White, green, and blue hangings are described. Royal display fills the scene before Esther herself is named.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-60-1-p:
First Peter in the King James text, starts with Peter, an apostle of Christ, writing to strangers scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. They are elect by God's foreknowledge, through sanctification of the Spirit.

Obedience and sprinkling of Christ's blood are named, with grace and peace multiplied to them. Peter blesses God, who by abundant mercy has begotten them again to a lively hope through Christ's resurrection. Their inheritance is incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven, while they are kept by God's power through faith. Joy under trial follows at once.
the-blue-flower:
Henry Van Dyke opens The Blue Flower with a long preface on how his short tales came to be one book. He says the tales grew side by side like blooms on one bush, not like goods packed in a box. The first of them, the tale of The Other Wise Man, came to him at least ten years before the rest were set down.

Van Dyke says he wrote of the inner life, and that such work needs time, rain, and plain tasks. He sought the right word, kept close to real life, and shunned stock ways of thought. The preface is frank about how small the fruit of long work can look, yet it claims that slow years add truth and worth to the tales that follow.
the-blunderer:
The Blunderer: or, The Counterplots is an English form of Molière's five-act verse play L'Étourdi. A long note says it was first played at Lyons in 1653 and reached Paris in November 1658, where it won great praise. The note traces much of the plot to an Italian play by Nicolo Barbieri, with bits from Fabritio de Fornaris, Luigi Grotto, Plautus, and Noël du Fail.

At the heart of the piece stands Mascarille, the quick-witted servant who drives the plot. The note calls him the first true new figure Molière made, not a stock valet from old plays. He is free and bold, loose in his plans, and quick to dream up a new trick when one fails. Around him the note sets the braggart captain type and the paired fools of the Italian stage.
the-body-snatcher:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this tale of grave robbing in 1884, in his Tales and Fantasies set. Its roots lie in the true case of Burke and Hare, the Edinburgh corpse thieves. Med schools of that age paid cash for fresh corpses, no questions asked of the men who brought them.

Two med men buy corpses from a sly rogue and ask no tales of where they came from. Years on, a corpse on the slab turns out to be a man one of them knew in life. The tale is a short, grim peak of horror on the sins of a trade.
the-border-boys-across-the-frontier: Fremont B. Deering wrote The Border Boys Across the Frontier, put out in New York by the A. L. Burt Company with rights dated 1911 from Hurst and Company. The first parts track a haunted mesa, a sand storm, a night alarm, and queer tracks. A hollow altar, the tale of a lost race, and the mesa folk's burial ground come next. Gun-runners and Madero's flying column close the parts shown.
the-boy-trapper: Harry Castlemon wrote The Boy Trapper, put out in Philadelphia by Henry T. Coates and Company. The pages shown are lists of Castlemon's own sets, not the tale. His Gunboat set has six books, from Frank the Young Naturalist to Frank on the Prairie. The Boy Trapper set also has three: The Buried Treasure, The Boy Trapper, and The Mail-Carrier. A plate caption names a meeting: Dave meets Lester Brigham. The Frank Nelson set holds Snowed Up, Frank in the Forecastle, and The Boy Traders.
the-burning-spear-being-the-experiences-: John Galsworthy wrote The Burning Spear, the experiences of Mr. John Lavender in the time of war, recorded under initials. A note by the producer says Galsworthy called the book revenge of the nerves, a thing born of the dreads and griefs of war. A verse from Tom O'Bedlam stands at the front, of a burning spear and a horse of air in the wilderness. The contents list eleven parts, each named by number alone.
the-cabman-s-story-the-mysteries-of-a-lo:
The Cabman's Story: The Mysteries of a London Growler starts on a family holiday. Rain threatened, and Fanny was just coming round from the whooping cough, so a four-wheeler was hired. The party rides from Hammersmith to the Alexandra Palace. Wife, sister-in-law, Tommy, Fanny, and Jack fill the inside. The narrator climbs up beside the driver with his waterproof.

The driver is a knowing old veteran with a weather-beaten face and white side whiskers. Asked if a hansom would pay better, he grants it would, but scorns the trade. A four-wheeler is a respectable conveyance, and its driver a respectable man; money is not to be compared to position. He has saved his little penny, and after forty-seven years on the streets he will begin and end on a growler.
the-case-of-general-ople-and-lady-camper:
The Case of General Ople and Lady Camper, by George Meredith, opens with the retired general house-hunting beyond the suburbs of London. An excursion planned since his retirement takes him across a famous common. It leads to a lofty highway along a park's borders. Then it comes within a stone's throw of the river. There he means not only to settle. He means to bestow his affections for life.

His daughter Elizabeth is eighteen and about to manage his house. She restrains his impulse to take the first place seen. Fortune guides them to a small estate. It has a lodge like two sentry-boxes forced into union. A back drive and stables complete it. Meredith's comedy begins in the general's own vocabulary: the house is bijou for a week, then, as contentment works on it, a gentlemanly residence.
the-case-of-the-registered-letter:
The Case of the Registered Letter, by Augusta Groner, translated by Grace Isabel Colbron, opens with the standing introduction to Joe Muller, the Austrian secret service detective of these tales. Unlike Holmes or Lecoq, Muller is small, slight, plain, and retiring, a man of indefinite age whose modesty is his chief characteristic.

The introduction gives that modesty a history. A wrongful conviction in his youth brought years in prison. A stigma then made honest work impossible. It drove him to live by his peculiar talents in the police. Bureaucratic etiquette still ranks him barely above a policeman, though the department realises its treasure and kings consult him. Content with a simple income and the work itself, Muller is presented complete before the registered letter enters the story.
the-cavalier: George W. Cable wrote this novel, dated 1901 on its title page. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing thirty-five chapters. Their titles name Lieutenant Ferry, Coralie Rothvelt, Charlotte Oliver, a fight on a bridge, and a charge in a lane.Readers must take the book on its title page alone.
the-century-vocabulary-builder: Garland Greever and Joseph M. Bachelor wrote this handbook in the Century Handbook Series, dedicated to Dana H. Ferrin. Only the series list, title page, and the start of the contents are present here. The first two chapters promise reasons for growing one's word stock, then a study of words in combination and their pitfalls.The front matter is all a reader gets in this record.
the-child-s-world-third-reader: Hetty S. Browne, Sarah Withers, and W. K. Tate prepared this third reader in the Child's World series, published by the Johnson Publishing Company of Richmond, Virginia. Only the title pages and a list of teachers' aids are present here, offering reading charts, a manual for the first five grades, and word cards.Front matter alone is a thin basis, and it is all there is.
the-christmas-dinner:
Shepherd Knapp wrote this Christmas play, issued at Philadelphia in 1921 by the Heidelberg Press. He dedicates it to those who first acted in it, to the trainers who drilled them with skill and patience, and to the friendly audiences of boys and girls. The piece is plainly built for young players and school stages.

The first scene opens the curtain on a farmhouse kitchen, just as Mother Goose promised. A fireplace with a mantel shelf stands at the back, a bright fire burning, with a lit lamp and an unlit candle on the shelf. A cupboard, a wood box, a broom, and a dustpan fill out the set. Grandfather and Grandmother sit in comfortable chairs, one on each side of the fire. The staging directions run in plain present tense, so a small company can build the room from household goods and follow the action with ease.
the-cinema-murder:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this mystery, dated 1917, opening Book I at a small country station. The afternoon train from London grinds into Detton Magna with much fuss and steam. An elderly porter puts on his coat and comes out of the small red-brick lamp room on his usual hopeless errand.

The station master scans the closed, streaming windows with an expectancy dulled by daily disappointment. Passengers seldom alight here, and this day breaks no record. One young man steps onto the wet, flinty platform and hands over half of a third-class return ticket from London. He wears no overcoat, turning up the collar of a well-worn blue serge coat against the rain. He climbs the long ascent into town through a cheerless landscape. Oppenheim sets a drab arrival before the cinema crime of the title enters.
the-compleat-angler:
Izaak Walton's discourse of fish and fishing opens with a letter of dedication to John Offley of Madeley Manor in Staffordshire, his most honored friend. Walton asks that Offley's patronage and protection cover the book. He rests the request on their shared ground: Offley knows angling well, and both loves and practices it.

Angling is an art, Walton insists, whatever ignorant men of another belief may say, and Offley knows that art better than others. The proof lies in the pleasant labor Offley enjoys when he gives his mind rest from serious business and gives a day or two to the recreation. Common anglers watching his success, Walton argues, would feel emulation, and emulation might breed diligent effort. Yet such skill, he grants, is not attainable by common capacities.
the-complete-essays-of-charles-dudley-wa: Charles Dudley Warner's complete essays appear here in a Backlog Edition within his complete writings, dated 1904. Only a contents list of the entire volume is present here, naming As We Were Saying, Rose and Chrysanthemum, The Red Bonnet, Social Screaming, The Directoire Gown, and many more short pieces. Later titles treat women in Congress, dinner-table talk, the burden of Christmas, and the responsibility of writers.Beyond the front matter, nothing is present to describe.
the-confessions-of-a-beachcomber:
E. J. Banfield wrote these confessions of an island life in tropical Queensland, with a Thoreau motto at the head about hearing a different drummer. He dedicates the book to the Honourable Robert Philp, M.L.A., praising his exact life and extensive charity. Banfield says he owes Philp much of his love for tropical Queensland.

The contents map a settler's world in three parts. Part I opens with the beachcomber's domain, an official landing, the island itself, and its early history, then satellites and neighbours. A second chapter treats beachcombing, tropical industries, island differences, and island fauna. A third turns to birds and their rights, with a census, a daybreak fugue, the megapode, and the swamp pheasant. Banfield writes as a resident naturalist, mixing practical island economy with close watching of birds and beaches.
the-conqueror-being-the-true-and-romanti: Gertrude Franklin Atherton calls her book The Conqueror, the true and romantic story of Alexander Hamilton. The Macmillan edition was first published in March 1902. A line from Talleyrand heads the book, ranking Hamilton above Napoleon and Fox. Atherton thanks James Bryce and Dr. Allan McLane Hamilton, without whose urging she would not have tried to recreate the statesman she calls the greatest of America's. The contents open with Nevis and Book I on Rachael Levine. Only front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-5-may-1:
May 1862 brings the fifth number of The Continental Monthly, devoted to literature and national policy. Its lead piece, What Shall We Do With It?, draws a parallel between the present war with the South and the American struggle against Britain a century before.

Just as few colonists at first sought independence, the writer says, the North took up arms to defend the Constitution and the Union, not to end slavery. Yet events push emancipation forward: slaves free themselves as armies advance and masters flee. Congress has barred troops from returning those who flee bondage, and the President has proposed federal aid for states that free their slaves. What began as an afterthought, he argues, is becoming the war's prime object.
the-cost-of-shelter: Ellen H. Richards, instructor in sanitary chemistry at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, published The Cost of Shelter in 1905. The book opens by listing why a household exists: shelter against the outside world, raising children, a shared life, company, independence, or suiting one's own tastes. Its contents treat the house in family life and as a mark of social standing. They treat the harm done by homes inherited from the 1800s that no longer fit changed conditions. Only this opening matter and part of the contents are present here.
the-cow-puncher: Robert J. C. Stead, author of The Homesteaders, The Bail Jumper, and Songs of the Prairie, wrote The Cow Puncher, published in Toronto by the Musson Book Company under a Canadian copyright of 1918. Its contents list twenty numbered chapters with no titles given. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the tale itself does not appear.
the-cruise-of-the-dazzler: Jack London's The Cruise of the Dazzler, dated 1902, is shown here only through its contents, headed by James E. West, Chief Scout Executive. The chapter titles trace a boy's path from home and examination day to Frisco Kid, the bay pirates, and the oyster-beds. They run from Brother and Sister and The Biter Bitten to Aboard the Dazzler. Joe Tries to Take French Leave and Frisco Kid Tells His Story close the list. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-crystal-stopper: Maurice LeBlanc's The Crystal Stopper, dated 1912, is shown here only through its contents, which list thirteen chapters. The titles move from The Arrests and Eight from Nine Leaves One through The Home Life of Alexis Daubrecq. They pass The Twenty-Seven, The Death-Sentence, and The Profile of Napoleon. They end with The Scaffold and The Last Battle. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-dairyman-s-daughter:
Legh Richmond, author of The Annals of the Poor, wrote The Dairyman's Daughter in an Edinburgh edition from Alexander Hislop and Company. Chapter I opens with a statement of aim: it is a pleasant task to trace the work of divine grace in the lives of God's real children.

Richmond argues that faith shows its most simple and pure form among the poor, who are rich in belief, while riches, rank, and polished society lay many blocks in religion's way. The poor man's cottage, he says, is often the palace of God. The tale ahead, he promises, is drawn from real life and circumstance, and begins with a letter he transcribes from the original before him.
the-dark-flower:
John Galsworthy divides The Dark Flower into three parts named Spring, Summer, and Autumn. A verse from The Bard of the Dimbovitza stands at the front, begging a lover to take the flower from breast and hair and go, since the night is fair.

Part I, Spring, opens on a youth walking along Holywell one afternoon in early June, his short gown drooping from his arms, and no cap on his thick dark hair. In 1880 that made him before his time. Built of two strains, sturdy and wiry, he has a strong face softened by a moody look, dark grey eyes that seem to gaze beyond what they see, and a swift smile. People stare as he passes; women note that he takes no notice of them, lost in plans for life after Oxford.
the-death-of-balder:
Johannes Ewald's Danish tragedy The Death of Balder, dated 1773, comes to English readers through George Borrow, author of Bible in Spain, Lavengro, and Wild Wales. The London edition from Jarrold and Sons, dated 1889, was limited to two hundred and fifty copies. In a preface Borrow calls the tragedy, with the opera The Fishermen, Ewald's best work, the opera holding the bold lyric that became the national song of the Danes.

Borrow asks Danish readers to judge whether any thought or turn in his version lacks its match in the original. He kept the peculiar blank verse of the Danish, he says, so English readers could form an exact idea of it, even at some cost in grace. The persons are Balder, Hother, Thor, Nanna, Loke, and three Valkyries, and the scene is a pine-wood on the Norwegian mountains under snow-topped rocks.
the-deerslayer:
James Fenimore Cooper opens The Deerslayer under a verse from Childe Harold praising the pathless woods and the lonely shore. Before the tale starts, he reflects that events work on the imagination like time: a history rich in incidents soon takes on the air of great age.

American annals already look venerable, he says, yet four ordinary lifetimes, passing word from mouth to mouth, could span all that civilized man has done within the republic. Little more than two centuries have passed since the Dutch began settling what became New York. Settlements on the eastern shore of the Hudson, such as Claverack, Kinderhook, and even Poughkeepsie. They were not thought safe from Indian attack a century ago, a fact meant to set the reader in the right frame for the pictures ahead.
the-depot-master: Joseph C. Lincoln's The Depot Master is shown here only through its contents, which list eighteen chapters. The titles mix small-town color with incident. Among them are At the Depot, Stingy Gabe, The Major, A Baby and a Robbery, and Aviation and Avarice. The Widow Bassett, The Great Metropolis, The Hero and the Cowboy, and The Cruise of the Red Car follow. Only the title page, contents, and the heading of Chapter I are present here.
the-deserter:
Richard Harding Davis's The Deserter, printed by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1918 with an introduction by John T. McCutcheon, opens in Salonika. The American consul, the Standard Oil man, and the war correspondents form the American colony there, waiting to go to the front while the front comes rapidly toward them.

Among them are Uncle Jim, the veteran of many wars, oldest in experience and youngest in spirit. The Kid boasts he is the only boy reporter to jump from a City Hall assignment to a European war. The Kid scorns strategy writing: the man at home wants human interest, heart-to-heart talks about refugees and wounded, and how to pronounce Salonika. The third man is John, the special artist, whose front-page cartoons made him famous.
the-diamond-master:
Jacques Futrelle, author of Elusive Isabel and The Thinking Machine, wrote The Diamond Master, published in Indianapolis by the Bobbs-Merrill Company in 1909 with pictures by Herman Pfeifer. Its contents promise more and more diamonds, an unlimited supply, a mysterious woman, a winged messenger, Mr. Czenki, and a great cube.

Chapter I, The First Diamond, opens on the morning mail of the head of a great business house. It holds thirty or forty personally addressed letters, and a plain package wrapped in yellow paper, about the size of a cigarette-box. The parcel is neatly tied with thin scarlet twine and bears no markings beyond a precise copperplate address and the smudge of the postmark.
the-doctor-s-daughter:
The Doctor's Daughter, a novel signed only Vera, author of Honor Edgeworth, opens with a long, arch preface. Vera jokes that prefaces, like whispered words when guests are named at a party, can win a fair hearing for a plain book. She owns she is no Dickens, and asks pardon for her book's rough looks.

Her tale then turns to its heroine and the world of a doctor's house. Dickens is her stated model for warmth and craft. The preface sets a tone of wit, modesty, and close watch on social rank.
the-dog-crusoe-and-his-master:
R. M. Ballantyne's tale The Dog Crusoe and His Master begins on the wild prairies watered by the Missouri River. Chapter one gives Crusoe's parentage and the pains of his puppyhood, when he was a soft, blind, squeaking pup. Past the far frontier live Pawnee, Sioux, Delaware, Crow, and Blackfeet peoples, with wild horses, deer, and buffalo.

Crusoe grows into a strong, famed dog at a backwoods settlement. His young master and he face hunts, camps, and perils in the West. Ballantyne wrote for boys, and the tale mixes fact, faith, and bold deeds.
the-dore-bible-gallery-complete-containi:
The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations, in its complete form, gathers one hundred plates by Gustave Doré with a page of story text before each cut. Its preface says the grand first work cost too much for most homes, so this cheaper volume picks the most famed events and persons of Scripture for a wide circle of readers.

Artists and scholars checked the work as it grew, the preface adds. Each plate gets a short narrative to set the scene. The set made Doré's bold, dark Bible scenes a fixture in homes that could never buy the folio.
the-dynamiter:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Fanny Van de Grift Stevenson wrote The Dynamiter as More New Arabian Nights, first issued in April 1885. This 1903 Longmans printing carries a wry dedication to two police officers, Cole and Cox. Crime, the authors say, is too ugly to treat in a grave spirit here; horror fits nobler sins.

Linked tales follow a young man through London's dynamite scares, with Fenian plots, disguises, and chance. The tone stays light while bombs tick. Stevenson turns terror into a game of tales told in clubs and lodgings. Chance meetings bind the chain of tales.
the-editor-s-relations-with-the-young-co:
William Dean Howells writes on the editor and the young contributor in this piece from Literature and Life. He mocks the old joke that editors live in dread of young writers. His own years at the desk taught him the reverse: a magazine lives only by new blood, and the editor longs for fresh voices, new scenes, and the breath of morning.

Odds still weigh hard against the young, he owns. Howells, once dean of American letters, counsels both sides with grace. The essay shows how the great magazines of his age picked their voices.
the-elements-of-character:
Mary G. Chandler's The Elements of Character, dated 1854, opens with a warning drawn from the Edinburgh Review. Schooling of mind alone breeds hard hearts. Schooling of feeling alone breeds folly. Schooling of faith alone can end in madness or unbelief. Chandler sets her book for her old pastor, E. H. Sears, under whose care her mind learned to dwell on sacred themes.

Her contents name character, thought, imagination, affection, life, talk, manners, and company. Each part asks how a soul takes shape. The book is a calm New England guide to the making of a good person.
the-empire-of-austria-its-rise-and-prese:
John S. C. Abbott's The Empire of Austria; Its Rise and Present Power, printed at New York in 1859, belongs to his Monarchies of Continental Europe set. Its first heads trace the Habsburgs from Albert, Count of Hapsburg, through Rhodolph's marriage, estates, and clash with the Church, to his election as Emperor of Germany and a bishop's warning.

Abbott wrote swift, tale-like history for home readers. Baron confederacies, mountain passes, and crowned heads fill his pages. The book tracks one family's rise from a castle to a vast, mixed empire at Europe's heart.
the-enchanted-typewriter:
John Kendrick Bangs's The Enchanted Typewriter claims a strange birth: for six months, from midnight to four, unseen hands worked an old typewriter in his library corner. Bangs found the machine, a relic of the early seventies, while laid up with grip and poking through his attic's old books, letters, and boyhood stuff. How it came there, he cannot recall.

The unseen typist proves to be a spirit from the dead past, keen on fresh gossip of earth. Bangs frames the tales as late-night dictation. Wit and ghost lore mix in his light, chatty style.
the-end-of-the-tether:
Joseph Conrad's The End of the Tether opens aboard the steamer Sofala as she turns for a low, swampy coast. Sunlight shatters on the calm sea into a blaze that tires the eye. Captain Whalley stands mute while his Serang, a small, alert Malay, murmurs the helm orders in his place. Whalley does not speak even to steady the helm.

Whalley is going blind and hides it to keep his post and his daughter's income. Pride, age, and a rogue partner grind him down. Conrad's late tale of the eastern seas is grave, slow, and unsparing.
the-everlasting-whisper:
Jackson Gregory's The Everlasting Whisper, a tale of the California wilderness, opens in Sierra springtime. Ridges sweep down to the hot, brown Sacramento Valley on one side and up to snow-capped crests on the other, so winter, spring, and ripe summer touch across seventy miles. Snow still grips the heights at seven thousand feet while fruit drops below.

An old prospector's secret and a girl raised in the wilds draw men into the high timber. Gregory sets the tale for Maxwell E. Perkins, his famed editor. Gold, love, and the call of the hills drive it.
the-expedition-of-humphry-clinker:
Tobias Smollett's The Expedition of Humphry Clinker opens as letters about letters. Writing to a London bookseller from Abergavenny on August 4, the sender answers word that his friend the Rev. Hugo Behn has handed over a bundle of private mail. The bookseller sees good sales in print but fears suits from folk still living whose words would be laid bare.

No secrecy sealed the letters, the sender pleads, and no one's name is harmed. The tale that follows tracks Matthew Bramble's cranky tour of spas and towns. Smollett's last novel is his warmest and funniest.
the-experiences-of-a-bandmaster:
John Philip Sousa's The Experiences of a Bandmaster looks back on eighteen years of playing for the masses: twelve in United States service and six before the general public. As conductor of the Marine Band, he played at White House state functions. He saw much of its social life at close range. He served under five presidents: Hayes, Garfield, Arthur, Cleveland, and Harrison. All were keen on music, he says.

He jokes that Grant knew but two tunes, one being Yankee Doodle. Tales of presidential whims, tours, and mishaps follow. The March King's own prose is brisk, warm, and full of band-room lore.
the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher:
Edgar Allan Poe opens this tale with a ride across a bleak tract of land on a dull, dark day in autumn. The narrator draws near the melancholy House of Usher and feels a gloom he cannot shake or name.

He studies the bare walls, the blank windows like eyes, the rank sedges, and the white trunks of dead trees. Even the view in the black tarn below doubles the dread. He has come to stay some weeks with Roderick Usher, a boyhood friend whose letter begged him to come. House and family share one name, and both seem near their fall.
the-field-of-clover:
Laurence Housman wrote The Field of Clover as a book of fairy tales, with wood carving by his sister Clemence Housman. This Dover printing of 1968 copies the first edition of 1898 word for word.

The longest tale, The Bound Princess, runs in six parts, from fire-eaters and a galloping plough to a camphor worm. Shorter tales follow: The Crown's Warranty, The Wishing-Pot, The Feeding of the Emigrants, and The Passionate Puppets. Housman twists old fairy forms into odd, sly shapes, where wishes, spells, and proud folk meet strange ends in green fields and small kingdoms.
the-field-of-ice-part-ii-of-the-adventur:
Jules Verne's The Field of Ice forms part two of the Captain Hatteras tale, and this copy matches the Routledge printing of 1875 noted at its head. The same early English rendering, with no translator named, is used here.

The head note lists other English versions from Boston and London, and says this early work never won the wide fame of Verne's later books. The story goes on with the polar crew, the doctor's stores, and Altamont's first words. Two records in this set hold the same front matter and text, word for word, so far as can be read here.
the-flamingo-feather: Kirk Munroe wrote The Flamingo Feather as a tale of old Florida. It was first printed in 1887 and again under his copyright in 1915. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads name Rene de Veaux and a youth named Has-se. Has-se is held prisoner. A mutiny at Fort Caroline and the coming of Jean Ribault stand in the list. All this points to a boy's tale of the French in Florida. Their wars with Spain and the tribes fill the ground.
the-fortune-hunter:
David Graham Phillips wrote The Fortune Hunter as a novel of a smooth fraud in New York, built around a German actor named Feuerstein. Twelve chapters carry him from entry to exit.

Feuerstein leaves his East Sixteenth Street boarding house one April day, dressed with care: long coat, pearl-gray hat set at a bold tilt. He looks the romantic hero and knows it. Phillips shows a man with no money and grand airs hunting a rich wife, sure that brass beats gold. Women find him charming, men find him a threat, and his climb ends in a sharp fall.
the-gambler:
Fyodor Dostoyevsky wrote The Gambler as a novel set in a German spa town he calls Roulettenberg, turned into English by C. J. Hogarth. A young tutor tells the tale in his own voice.

The tutor comes back from two weeks away to find the General's household in a strange mood: cold pride, hints of new money, and shame behind the show. Polina, the General's stepdaughter, treats him with cool distance that hides a bond. Guests from France and England gather for fine dinners while the wheel spins nearby. Love, pride, and the lust for a win pull the whole house toward the tables.
the-gentle-grafter:
O. Henry wrote The Gentle Grafter as tales of Jeff Peters, a kind-hearted con man of the American road. Fourteen tales make up the book, told by Peters to a straight-faced friend.

The first tale, The Octopus Marooned, opens with a claim by Peters. A trust, he says, is weakest at one point. His friend calls the remark a riddle. Peters calls it an epitogram and spins his yarn. Through the set he poses as a healer, a college chair, and a matchmaker. He fleeces the greedy by a rough code. He never cheats an honest man who does not want something for nothing.
the-ghost-of-jerry-bundler: W. W. Jacobs and Charles Rock made The Ghost of Jerry Bundler as a play from Jacobs' tale Jerry Bundler. The play stands under a copyright of 1908. Only the front matter is present here, and it is all stage law. It sets royalty terms of five dollars a show for amateur use. It warns on rights at length. It rules that each program must credit Samuel French of New York. No scene or speech of the play shows up in these pages.
the-golden-chersonese-and-the-way-thithe: Isabella L. Bird wrote The Golden Chersonese and the Way Thither. She is also named as Mrs. Bishop. Only front matter is present here. It is a Project Gutenberg header. The header gives notices on copyright laws. It tells readers to keep the file whole. It honors the volunteers who made the text. No page of the travel book itself is present. Nothing about the trip, the lands seen, or the route taken can be told from what is here.
the-great-big-treasury-of-beatrix-potter:
Beatrix Potter wrote The Great Big Treasury of Beatrix Potter. It gathers her tales in one volume. A contents list names nineteen pieces. They run from The Tale of Peter Rabbit and The Tailor of Gloucester through The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck. They end with The Tale of Mr. Tod and The Tale of Pigling Bland.

The first tale, Peter Rabbit, opens in the classic words. Once upon a time there were four little rabbits. Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter are their names. Home is a sand-bank under the root of a very big fir tree, where they live with their mother. One morning old Mrs. Rabbit speaks to them. They may go into the fields or down the lane, she says. But they must not go into Mr. McGregor's garden. That warning, and Peter's fate, start the most famous of these animal tales.
the-great-hunger:
Johan Bojer wrote The Great Hunger. W. J. Alexander Worster and C. Archer translated it from the Norwegian. Book I opens on a Norwegian fjord. For sheer havoc, the book says, no gale matches a good northwester. It roars through the long winter evenings and churns the water to froth. Boats are flung in somersaults to the doors of the fisher huts.

Against that storm the book sets a calm spring day. At low water a wonderland lies bare. Urchins splash in clear pools among the rocks. On such a day two boys of fourteen hurry from a fisher's hut to the beach. Peer Troen is fair-haired and sallow-faced. He pushes a wheelbarrow. Martin Bruvold, dark and freckled, carries a tub. Both whisper, up to some mischief. Peer, as always, is the ringleader.
the-guilty-river:
Wilkie Collins wrote The Guilty River. A contents list names eighteen chapters. They run from On the Way to the River and The River Introduces Us. They run through He Shows Himself, He Explains Himself, and He Betrays Himself. They name The Deaf Lodger and Gloody Settles the Account. They end with The Mistress of Trimley Deen.

Chapter I opens on a summer evening. The narrator has excused himself from a dinner-party at his stepmother's wish. He prefers to be alone, catching insects. With a brush and a mixture of rum and treacle, he goes into Fordwitch Wood. He paints the tree trunks with the mixture, in the practice called sugaring the trees.
